AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PENALTIES AND TREATMENT
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-40, to amend the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PENALTIES AND TREATMENT
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PENALTIES AND TREATMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to distinguish between the user and non-user of drugs with respect to trafficking. By providing the death penalty or life imprisonment for the non-user trafficking in drugs it is hoped that this will be a strong deterrent in the case of the trafficker who operates on the basis of business risk and economic returns. Increased penalties and rigid enforcement have been found to be strong deterrents in other countries faced with the problem.
The second step, once having stopped or curtailed the supply of drugs, is to try to effect a cure of the user by compulsory treatment. Since the majority of provinces are not in a position to provide the treatment and cure at present, proclamation can be made when the facilities are acquired in each province for that specific province, or proclamation of the treatment section may be made when all the provinces have facilities for the treatment and cure of users.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY AND METHOD OF EXECUTION
AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY AND METHOD OF EXECUTION
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-41, to amend the Criminal Code (capital punishment) .

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY AND METHOD OF EXECUTION
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY AND METHOD OF EXECUTION
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to provide the death penalty for those crimes coming within the definition of capital murder. In general, this legislation seeks to exclude from the death penalty those crimes generally referred to as crimes of passion, but retains the death penalty as a deterrent where 79951-0-39J
a murder occurs during a theft or as a result of the use of an offensive weapon or by an explosion. The bill seeks to protect police officers, prison guards and those assisting them by using the death penalty as a deterrent to prevent murder while these persons acting in the course of their duty or those assisting them seek to arrest a person or retain a prisoner in custody. In the case of treason and a person convicted of two or more murders, the death penalty is also applied.
Instead of execution by hanging, provision is made for execution by means of the gas chamber. The form of the traditional death sentence that a person shall "be hanged by the neck until he is dead" is changed so that the person shall "suffer death in the manner authorized by law". Provision is also made for disposal of the body either by burial, which is the present method, or by cremation.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Statement by Mr. Speaker fourth edition, there is commentary on page 147, citation 171, which reads in part as follows:
In putting a question a member must confine himself to the narrowest limits. In making a question, observations which might lead to debate cannot be regarded as coming within the proper limits of a question.

Those comments on our practice I think are reasonably clear, and they apply not only to questions which are asked but to the answers. On the Israeli-Syrian border, as hon. members know, there have been certain clashes in which unfortunately nationals of both sides have been killed. The United Nations emergency force has no jurisdiction with respect to that particular border, but there is a United Nations truce supervision organization on which Canada has 12 to 17 officers serving and which, of course, will be responsible for doing whatever is possible to bring about a settlement on that border.
On the southern border there have only been reports of Egyptian troops moving toward the border. speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, February 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Emilien Morissette for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. M. T. McDonald (Hamilton South):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Before beginning my remarks I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn) on his appointment as Deputy Speaker of this house. I know he will do a very fine job, as he has always done in the past. I should also like to congratulate the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Walker) on his appointment to the ministry. I am sure the new Minister of Public Works will put a little inspiration into his department as he did into the public accounts committee last year. I should also like to say that I believe the new Associate Minister of National Defence, the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Sevigny), will look after his duties in an exemplary way. Further, I should like to take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Morissette) on his remarks when proposing the address, and to say that I read them with great care. Finally I should like to commend the seconder of the motion, the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman), whose face has brought a little colour into the House of Commons.
I was very happy to see in the speech from the throne, that amendments to the Combines Investigation Act will be brought before the House of Commons this session. I believe there is a very definite need for this act to be amended so as to protect the interests of the small businessman against such things as loss leader selling, about which I will have the opportunity to speak further when the question comes up for discussion.
It is also very gratifying for me to see that the cities of Nanaimo and Oshawa will be the given new harbour commissions. I know if those two cities look after their harbours as well as the harbour commission of Hamilton has done through the co-operation of this government they will derive much benefit from the harbours not only in terms of free grants from the federal government and assistance in dredging, but by taking advantage of loans that may be forthcoming from this government to make possible the mass development of harbours throughout Canada.
It is also gratifying to see that this government is taking some action in the field of social legislation with respect to the social 79951-0-40
The Address-Mr. R. M. T. McDonald security act and the Veterans Allowance Act, to enable these folks to collect their pensions when living outside the country.
I am not going to talk at a great length about political expediency, because I have heard enough of that during the last eight or nine days, but will make just one refence of that nature. I read the budget speech made by Hon. Walter Harris on March 14, 1957, forecasting a buoyant economy for Canada. He told us we never had it so good and that everything was in a buoyant position. This was his two cups of coffee a day budget for our pensioners, a very loose type of thing. When he spoke he forgot one thing. He apparently forgot that he had on his desk at the time he spoke a report known as sessional paper No. 227, the economic outlook for 1957. While he was saying all these things about our buoyant economy he must have had on his desk as the then minister of finance a copy of that report.
What I want to talk abouf today is housing in general in Canada. I would point out that in this economic report for 1957 there were some cogent references to housing and the money market in the country at that time. I wish to place a section of this report on record. It reads as follows:
Housing construction is expected to drop fairly markedly below the high levels of the two previous years. The carryover into 1957 is much less than in recent years, and both starts and completions are expected to be down as well. The decline in activity in the current winter will be much more than seasonal, and a drop in the volume of roughly one fifth has been allowed for in the estimates.
That does not sound to me like a description of a buoyant housing program coming up in 1957. But this is the worst thing. Under the provisions of the National Housing Act there is a seotion which allows the federal government to get into the direct lending business. Here was a perfect opportunity for the then minister of finance to forecast that the government of that day would do something in the way of making increased funds available for housing, but he did not do this. When this government came into power on June 10, 1957, we found that the cupboard was bare as far as housing money was concerned.
The Liberals knew when they were in office that the lending institutions did not have sufficient money, so they should have taken the opportunity to put money into the housing market so that in the early spring money would have been available to make possible a complete housing construction program across the country. But they did not choose to do this. It is gratifying to note that since July 14, 1957 until today this government has made available $1,500 million

The Address-Mr. R. M. T. McDonald under the National Housing Act for direct lending, much more than the $150 million maximum allowed by the former government.
I should like to discuss for a few moments the different types of housing programs in which the federal government participates, including land assembly and the many other fields in which the federal government is engaged. In my own riding of Hamilton South we have 1300 government rental projects. The federal government puts up 75 per cent of this money and 25 per cent is put up by the provincial government. The administration of the houses comes under municipal jurisdiction. I should like to see a further development of this type of housing, but not too extensive. I think it is better to go into a limited dividend housing project than a complete program of rental housing across the country; because it would accomplish the same end.
It may be pointed out that in 1946 the federal government went into the limited dividend housing field. Between 1946 and the end of May of 1957, ten days prior to our coming into office, the federal government had put $58 million into limited dividend housing and apartments. It is interesting to observe that from June 10,	1957 until
December 31, 1959 this government in its two and a half years in power put 100 per cent more money into this field, an amount of $115 million, which I am sure has been of assistance across the nation and especially in my own community, where at the present time we have 300 rental apartments going up under the limited dividend scheme, as well as many homes for senior citizens.
The limited dividend scheme in my opinion should be in wider use across the country. This is an area where free enterprise can take a forthright stand. As hon. members may or may not know, one who builds a limited dividend apartment project is allowed only 5 per cent on his investment. When you see some of these individuals whom socialists would probably call capitalists going into this type of venture and collecting only 5 per cent on their investment, it convinces you that we have people on the capitalist side of the fence who are interested in looking after the interests of the little man in the country.
I might explain that the limited dividend apartment projects in my constituency provide accommodation for people with annual incomes ranging between $2,800 and $3,600. I am sure the government's stand in providing this type of mortgage money through private enterprise will achieve a better and more economical job. This type of lending is controlled by the government. The private individual cannot increase the rent by rule of

thumb. He is controlled in the rentals by the cost of land and construction all the way down the line. He has to have a government audit during construction. I have heard it said in my own constituency that free enterprisers under this scheme would gouge the construction costs and feather their own beds with thousands of dollars, but Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are not as stupid as that. They send out investigators to audit the books of the chief contractor and all the subcontractors on any such projects.
I should like to make a few suggestions. In examining some of the regulations under the limited dividend section of the National Housing Act it is very difficult to assess who needs a home and who does not. One instance comes to my mind of a man with five children who went to one of the developments in Hamilton and wanted to rent a three bedroom apartment. His income was $4,160 a year. Under the regulations three bedroom apartments are rented to people with a maximum income of $3,650, and when your income increases to approximately $4,600 or $4,700 you must vacate the apartment.
This is where a hardship is worked. We are trying to provide homes for people who need them. This man was paying $120 a month for his accommodation. I think some rule of thumb should be put into the regulations so that the man with a large family may obtain an apartment if his income does not exceed the limit at which he would be required to vacate. This is merely a suggestion. I think it should be arranged so that anyone who has more than three children could be allowed to earn $250 a year for each child in his family over three; thus the man with five children could have his income limit increased by $500, thus enabling him to take advantage of this type of accommodation.
It is also noted that the baby bonus is taken into consideration under the present regulations as far as income is concerned. I know of about 10 or 12 cases of Canadian people with large families, and who have incomes of $3,600 a year, are in this position. Because they have five children and are receiving a baby bonus of around $200 or $300 a year they are not given the privilege of moving into those houses. The inclusion of the baby bonus or the family allowance, or whatever you wish to call it, should be taken out of the regulations.
May I say that the limited dividend plan has been a great thing in helping the municipalities finance accommodation for senior citizens. I think the federal government has not gone far enough in this field. If the municipalities could band together with nonprofit organizations to look after the problem

I think the government should go all the way with them. As far as the limited dividend section is concerned, I know that in Hamilton an investigation was made by the contractors and city officials.
If free enterprise is expected to help the government in these low rental apartments I think the government should give them the opportunity right away to apply for mortgages. Under the regulations that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have set up they cannot accept applications from anyone if there is not any money in the kitty. I think it is time this regulation is changed so that anyone can apply. Putting in an application for a loan merely speeds up the process, and gives the person in the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation office a little time to peruse the application, so when the money is made available the application will be granted.
I should now like to deal with the section having to do with urban renewal and development. We have a great deal of this going on at the present time in my community. Unfortunately the city politicians are using it to get their names in the paper and have a little political fun, but it is a very important matter. Some two years ago in Hamilton an urban renewal study was done which showed that there were 10 blighted areas in the city which needed some renovation. If people in the communities in general across the country knew that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation would pay 75 per cent of the cost of any such study they would take advantage of it. There is an urban redevelopment study which is done by the municipality, 50 per cent of the cost of which comes under federal government and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation jurisdiction. After these studies are done it is up to the municipality to take action to acquire and clear the land.
In acquiring land the thought of expropriation always comes up. This is a very difficult thing. We have many such problems in Hamilton. Expropriation proceedings under the pertinent section of the National Housing Act do not come under the direct jurisdiction of the federal government. Not only the legal side of the picture should be looked at but also the moral side. In Hamilton some 31 homes of people who have lived in them for 30 years are being condemned. These people have been leasing the land for the past 30 years. Because they do not actually own the land they are going to be asked to move their homes after living in them for 30 odd years; they are asked to move them across a busy highway, which is a difficult thing to do.
79951-0-40i
The Address-Mr. R. M. T. McDonald
The city council of Hamilton should look not only at the legal aspects of this matter but at the moral aspects as well. This project is going to cost some $3 million. I think they should take a good look at this expropriation. It may be pointed out that after all this is being done under urban redevelopment, and that a proposal must be forthcoming to the federal government. Eight months ago members of the city council of Hamilton came to Ottawa to find out how far Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the Minister of Public Works would go in this development. They received a very good hearing, and several concessions pro and con were made and it looked as if we could go ahead and look after this situation. Eight months have gone by, but up to last week we had not received an application from the city of Hamilton. I hope the city will not come to the federal government in a couple of weeks with an application and want an answer in a week. They have waited some eight and one half months. I am sure that when they bring the application to us they will allow us a little time.
In the field of urban redevelopment I think it is the responsibility not only of the municipalities and the government but of the citizens to make themselves aware of what is going on in their community and to provide a proper housing and social structure in the blighted areas where crime is prevalent and poor housing conditions prevail.
My time is limited, but I should now like to talk about land assembly. I judge by some of the speeches of Liberal so-called backbenchers that they do not like land assembly. This is a subject on which hon. members can take different views, but I would like to suggest that I have learned something of land assembly in Hamilton in the last year. We had some 413 land assembly lots made available in my riding. These were not subsidized lots, as some of the Liberal members have stated; these were lots sold without profit.
I think there is something to be said about getting out of the land assembly business, but it must be done in a very careful way. The reason land assembly was first brought into the picture was to provide low cost serviced land for individuals who wanted to build houses. Low cost serviced land is a very fine thing to have. Municipalities are responsible first of all for putting in the services, but there seems to be a big gap in the co-operation of the municipalities and the federal government in this specific item. In Hamilton we have some 900 acres of land assembly property that could go on the market at any time in competition with free enterprise, builders and developers. We have heard the story of

The Address-Mr. R. M. T. McDonald the large investor who squeezes blood out of the people by getting high cost land and putting it on sale. I think that is quite true in certain localities. In Hamilton we have the builder-developer, not just the developer. I am proposing that the federal government get out of the land assembly business as such.
The current problems are many in Hamilton. We have some 250 builders, and we find that the 900 acres would give us approximately 4,500 lots which could be made available to the people in general. If the builders and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation would work together these lots could be made available in a systematic way. It is very bad policy on the part of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to dump 100 acres on the market right next to someone who might have property for which he paid $500 more.
I think the way to overcome this problem is to develop land on a systematic basis. Let us take the specific instance of Hamilton. Take the 250 builders and apportion to them the 4,500 lots at a below-market price. The market price in Hamilton for a 55-foot lot is somewhere around $4,700 or $4,800. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation officials could probably put a serviced lot on the market for about $3,300, which is well below the market value in Hamilton, and it would be a direct benefit to the person who brought the property.
I think this benefit could still be derived- on a mass basis if each of the builders had apportioned to him a number of lots, depending upon the type of construction he has undertaken in the past three or four years. They could build those houses as economically as an individual could build them himself. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation could put an end selling price on the houses. In other words, if the builder took advantage of the $3,300 lot, that $3,300 price would be below the market value and he would not be permitted to exploit the citizens of Hamilton and district by getting another $1,000 for the land in excess of what he paid for it. If the end price of the house was $15,000 or $15,500, then that would be the price the people of Hamilton would have to pay. It would still be a low cost house; they would still have low down payments because of the control over the selling price. I think C.M.H.C. officials, through the Minister of Public Works, should look at this problem very carefully and do it right away. I should' like to see this land assembly program in Hamilton carried out immediately, as there is a great problem with regard to servicing in the community.
There also comes to my mind the problem we are having with respect to senior citizens'


homes, and I think this is a perfect opportunity for Central Mortgage and Housing officials through the Minister of Public Works if they want to get on with land assembly in Hamilton. They could set aside 100 acres of this property almost by way of a grant to the community. I do not mean an outright grant, but if we are selling land at below market value I do not think it would hurt the people as a whole to add $100 or $200 to the cost of every acre being sold, so you would then have 100 acres that could be granted' almost free of charge to the municipality or to a nonprofit organization in order that they could build senior citizens' homes for not much more than the amount of mortgage they could get under the limited dividend scheme.
I know there is a great deal of discussion about interest rates and money today. I think we are all worried about the increase in interest rates, but I should like to take another view. The Minister of Public Works indicated that he would raise the interest rate from 6 per cent to 6| per cent on insured N.H.A. loans made by lending institutions, and I think it is the responsibility of these lending institutions to put forth a great effort to make money available at 6f-per cent. Their security is almost like a gilt-edged government bond, and when we are going through a rough financial period I think it is up to the lending institutions to get behind Canada and lend the money required so that 125,000 homes may be built.
I also feel that the long range government program with respect to mortgages should be looked at, and that the government should not be regarded as the great white father handing out money to the people. After the present slight economic instability has passed I think the government should examine the situation very closely with a view to getting out of the mortgage business generally. I believe the government should concern itself more with federal-provincial housing, limited dividend housing and small homes of the 1,050 square feet type.
In my opinion the government has shown good faith with regard to housing since taking office, and has not acted in a political manner. I do not think members of the opposition will say the government has not taken action in regard to housing, because it has. It has increased the amount available for direct lending from the $150 million the Liberals had in the coffers to $1,500 million. It has increased the amount available for insured N.H.A. loans from $4 billion to $6 billion. I am sure everyone will agree that the government has done a fine job so far as housing is concerned.

I should like to say again that it is up to the lending institutions of Canada-I am not talking primarily about the banks but the insurance and trust companies-to go ahead, put their shoulders to the wheel and help us get out of the tight money slump. I am sure if they do the people of Canada will not only be grateful but will place more savings with them so they will be able to lend more money in the future.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my remarks, I want to join previous speakers in congratulating both the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne (Mr. Morissette and Mrs. Casselman).
I should also like to congratulate you for the confidence which the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and all the hon. members extended to you in unanimously electing you Deputy Speaker of this house, and to wish you well.
I should like to comment, in particular, the following paragraph of the speech from the throne:
Canada's general economic position has greatly Improved during 1959 and the prospects for 1960 are favourable. The recurring problem of seasonal unemployment remains, however, but apart from this, expansion of production and employment has been general across the nation.
That paragraph covers three main ideas: on the one hand, the economic position has improved in 1959, and the prospects for 1960 are favourable; on the other hand, the problem of seasonal unemployment is still with us; and finally, expansion in production and employment has been general across the nation.
That paragraph, added to the several statements made by the Right Hon. Prime Minister and members of his government, both here and elsewhere, present the economic position of Canada as an extravagant picture of felicity and prosperity, hardly in keeping with the facts.
Foremost among those is unemployment. The latest statistics show that the number of unemployed in Canada has now reached 755,537, i.e. about 60,000 more than on December 31, 1959. Consequently, more than 12 per cent of the Canadian labour force is now unemployed.
How many hundreds of million dollars is the national production thus being deprived of? Are not those figures impressive enough, especially in a country which we are given
The Address-Mr. Eudes to believe is prosperous, to call the immediate attention of the government, whose leader, three years ago, promised that, as long as he would be Prime Minister, no man able to work would remain unemployed?
Is this really a case as is claimed, of seasonal and accidental phenomenon, worthy of no more than a passing reference in the speech from the throne, when we know that, in the last three years it has recurred persistently and that for several months a year it paralyses business and industry, and affects the welfare of millions of people?
In that cheerless picture, the province of Quebec stands out with about 37 per cent of the total number of unemployed, which means over 225,000 people, almost 25 per cent of them in Montreal.
One fortunate thing, in all this misfortune, is that social security measures established by previous Liberal administrations, such as family allowances, old age pensions, unemployment insurance benefits, at least provide the bare necessities to the unemployed.
In the 1957 elections the leader of the Conservative party promised workers he would increase unemployment insurance benefits, eliminate the waiting period and extend the benefit period to 52 weeks.
Between the 1957 and 1958 elections legislation was indeed passed extending the period of seasonal benefits. That was between two elections. However, the 1959 amendments neither removed nor even shortened the waiting period. As a result, a large proportion of the unemployed do not yet qualify for benefits, or have simply exhausted their benefits.
On the other hand, in order to provide about $23i million a year more for unemployed workers, both workers and employers must now pay into the unemployment insurance fund $80 million more per year than they did previously.
Despite that increase in contributions, the unemployment insurance fund, from December 31, 1956 to December 31, 1959, lost close to $500 million. From 1955 to 1956, the last year of Liberal administration, the fund had gained $36 million, reaching a total of $926,776,830. On December 31, 1958, the fund had gone down to $625,363,366, and on December 31, 1959, to $471,094,255, a drop of $150 million in a single year.
Government members seem quite unconcerned about the extreme seriousness of this vital problem. They do occasionally acknowledge its existence, stressing that it is only

The Address-Mr. Eudes temporary, and they shrug off their responsibility by explaining that present unemployment is the unavoidable result of the sad legacy left by the previous administration, the Liberals. A very sad legacy indeed, which left them, in June, 1957, with two billion dollars in the till.
It is about time that government members should get rid of this opposition complex and realize that for close to three years now they and they alone have been responsible for running the country.
The only solution they could think of to stop unemployment was a winter works program.
Last year's results showed up the inefficiency of this plan under which the federal government offers to pay municipalities 50 per cent of the cost of labour on wintertime projects. Now, because of the high cost of winter works, and the necessary use of expensive machinery, that 50 per cent actually represents no more than 10 to 12 per cent of the total costs. The harshness of our climate necessarily restricts the quantity, the nature and the choice of those projects. Lastly, the complex procedure that has to be gone through in order to obtain federal government assistance, i.e., drawing up by municipalities of plans and specifications that have to be submitted for approval to the provincial governments, negotiations between the provinces and the federal government, and the final acceptance by the latter, would require that such procedures be started at least several months before unemployment showed its ugly head. Such has unfortunately not been the case since the winter works program was established. As a matter of fact the federal government waited until autumn to offer its assistance. In any event, according to the estimates of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), the program for 1960, will procure work for only 34,000 unemployed, and temporary employment 34,000 out of the more than 750,000 unemployed.
It seems useless to criticize on the inefficiency of the only solution the government has come up with to check unemployment. Yet, the situation is critical. It is practically the same as in January 1959, when religious authorities in Montreal, who were rightly alarmed, drew the attention of their parishioners to the pastoral letter dated January 18, 1959, of which I shall sum up a few points which deserve serious consideration.
A serious study of our economic system is imperative.
Present conditions mean destitution for too many families, and seriously endanger the social


order. The idleness of able-bodied men who want work but cannot find any is abnormal and against natural law.
The government has the power and the duty to redirect the economy according to prevailing circumstances at each particular time, for the welfare of all.
The state must play a positive role.
Unemployment begets poverty, temptation arising from despair, and criminality. It imperils social order by breeding discontent, and bitterness towards society which is unable to make use of living forces eager to be put to work. Finally, it is a paradox in a country that is immensely wealthy and in full development.
Yes, it is a paradox too, that this unemployment should be accompanied by a series of phenomena that usually have no relation to it, but which, once coupled with it, nevertheless remain detrimental to the expansion of a sound, prosperous and vigorous economy.
Thus, in 1959, there has been a continued notable rise in the cost of living. This rise, which curtails exports and favours imports, is a factor which could seriously increase the deficit in our trade balance and international accounts.
This rise also affects our approach to statistics such as those on retail and wholesale sales.
The interest rates have gone up enormously. Despite this substantial increase, which should normally attract the lenders, money has become scare. Municipalities and school corporations can hardly borrow the money required for their expansion, and when they do find it, they have to pay exorbitant rates of interest. For instance, recently, the city of Montreal had to agree to a rate of 7.58 per cent in order to borrow $13 million.
Industry, and more particularly small enterprises, are stifled by the three plagues of our economy: unemployment, inflation and tight money.
We are apt to question the accuracy of statements made by government members on our record of prosperity when we see the hundreds of notices published each week in Montreal newspapers of forced sales by court order, assignments of property to creditors, and bankruptcies facing craftsmen, tradesmen and industrialists who, after years of struggle, despite the increasing success they had known until three years ago, are forced to admit their failure now to use their native ability for the welfare of the community. All this because of economic developments beyond their control.
I have not enough time to talk about our huge deficit.

Our international accounts deficit is increasing in spite of an inflow of foreign capital momentarily sufficient to offset it.
I must point out that, even with attractive interest rates, foreign investors are more and more reluctant to invest in Canada. That is because Europe has made a good recovery since the second world war. Economic activity is picking up, and capital invested in other countries in the past is kept there to maintain commercial efficiency. Europe is gradually relaxing tariff barriers on imports and this can only be harmful to Canadian exporters.
In 1959, the inflow of foreign capital was 10 per cent less than in 1958 and at the end of October 1958, our external trade deficit had increased by half a billion dollars.
According to figures supplied by the D.B.S., in 1958, the external debt of Canada increased by $1,600,000,000.
Economists throughout the world have often repeated that a country, no more than an individual, can live indefinitely on borrowed money.
If Canada is to remain master of its own destiny, it is imperative that its policy should take into account various economic factors, namely unemployment, inflation, tight money, reduction of foreign capital investments, problems in maintaining foreign markets, reduction of the national deficit. That inescapable responsibility rests with the government. People are anxiously awaiting its reply.
May I now be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to comment as briefly as possible on an extremely important statement made by the Prime Minister when speaking in this debate, on January 18 last.
He said in substance that it was necessary to obtain, during this session of parliament, agreement to an amendment to our constitution on a question of national importance, in order to remove the necessity of going to the United Kingdom parliament to amend our own constitution.
Like the one announcing the setting up of a Hoover-type royal commission, that statement really took the house by surprise; not because it contained any original idea or unexpected project, but of the way in which it was introduced.
The speech from the throne had been delivered by His Excellency the Governor General only four days before.
The Address-Mr. Eudes
Now, according to a solidly established parliamentary tradition, that speech briefly announces all important legislation the government will be submitting to parliament during the session opened by it.
No one can possibly claim that this statement on the amendment to the constitution is a matter of secondary importance in the government's mind. On the other hand, it is difficult to imagine that this was inadvertently omitted from the speech from the throne.
The fact remains that the announcement of this legislation was not contained in the speech from the throne. Why? It is contrary to the rules of this house to impute motives to an hon. member. However, one can still wonder. Why, for instance, was this legislation announced immediately after the Leader of the Opposition took part in the debate? Was this a piece of political strategy on the part of the Prime Minister? Nobody but himself will know.
Be that as it may, it seems like a strange procedure on the part of a man who, while he was in the opposition, and particularly during the election campaign of 1957, set himself up as the champion of the privileges and rights of parliament and its members.
This strange attitude of the Prime Minister towards respect for the rules and customs of the house is not an isolated case.
On this very matter, may I quote an editorial from Montreal's La Presse of January 29, 1960:
Almost three years ago, when the present Prime Minister of Canada sat in the opposition, he aroused people all across the country by denouncing the closure rule as an instrument of oppression, as a violation of the principle of free discussion in a democratic parliament. He most solemnly pledged himself to abolish this abominable parliamentary rule, if he was brought to power.
Mr. Diefenbaker was elected Prime Minister. Apparently faithful to his election promise, at the very first session of parliament following the 1957 election, he put on the order paper of the House of Commons a resolution for the removal of the closure provision from the rules of procedure. But -for there is a but-the session ended and the resolution remained on the order paper until the session ended and was never submitted to the approval of the house. During the 1958 and 1959 sessions, the matter was not brought up, nor was it in 1960. Answering a question put to him this week about it, he said parliament had more important and more urgent matters to look after.
He even added with complacency, not to say with arrogance, that this rule, also referred to as "the gag'', could be dangerous under a Liberal administration, but was not so under a Conservative government which guarantees the greatest freedom of discussion.
It's a rather rickety piece of logic, for even if the Prime Minister's explanation is taken literally, that is, if we admit, for argument's sake, that closure is dangerous under a Liberal administration and not so under a Conservative one, would

The Address-Mr. Eudes it not be elementary prudence for the present government to suppress it at once so that it would not be used by another party if there is a change of government?
If this rule of procedure is objectional per se, is it not dangerous to let it remain in the book. If there is no intention of using it, why keep it in force? Is it not likely to give the impression that it may come in handy in case it is considered necessary or opportune to apply it?
At all events, we must welcome the announcement of this legislation that will enable us to modify our constitution ourselves, without the consent of the United Kingdom's parliament. This power is an attribute still missing for our complete emancipation and for the absolute sovereignty of Canada.
Compared to Australia and New Zealand, we must admit that Canada is still dependent.
The act of the British parliament which, in July 1900, grouped the various Australian colonies under a confederation, gave Australia its constitution, and its people the power to amend it without recourse to Westminster.
The same thing happened in the case of New Zealand when that country became a dominion in 1907.
Mr. Paul Gerin-Lajoie, in his book "Constitutional amendment in Canada", says that very early after the adoption of the British North America Act this question of amending by ourselves of our own constitution came to certain minds. As early as 1883, the Toronto newspaper The Bystander said that this power should be the property of the nation. Such opinions were however considered extremist and even anti-imperialist.
In 1920, a noted British peer, Sir Clifford Sifton, described our method of amending the constitution as "an anachronism and an absurdity".
The matter was officially discussed in parliament for the first time in March 1920, by the then leader of the opposition, Mr. Mackenzie King on the occasion of a debate on the peace treaty with Bulgaria. Here is an excerpt from his statement.
(Text):
The government should consider the advisability of an address being presented to His Majesty to have powers given to the parliament of Canada, subject to the concurrence of the several provinces of the dominion, to amend the constitution of Canada in such particulars as may be agreed upon as a result of conference between the provincial and federal authorities and approved by this parliament and the legislatures of the different provinces.
(Translation):
We know that, in the meantime, especially since the imperial conference of 1926, the idea has spread far and wide. The problem gave rise to numerous studies and discussions. Throughout his long parliamentary career, the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe has kept
[Mr. Eudes.l
urging that constitutional reform. The ideas of our former prime minister, the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, on that question are well known.
Yet, in spite of the numerous federal-provincial conferences where the problem was considered, all efforts made in that connection have not yet given the desired result because a formula acceptable to each of the provinces and to the federal government has not yet been found.
This does not mean, however, that Canada considers itself in a state of subordination vis-a-vis the United Kingdom, but it hesitates in the fear it should lose its acquired rights, to accept such a constitutional change.
Nor should it be thought that the United Kingdom parliament is anxious to retain that prerogative. On the contrary, it is rather anxious to relinquish this rather embarrassing power which makes it the trustee and guardian of our constitution.
It would be premature at this stage to suggest an appropriate procedure.
Let us only note that the thinking on this matter has matured. If some machinery is suggested to enable us to amend our own constitution, and if this machinery takes into account both provincial and federal autonomy and racial, religious, cultural and regional factors, the project is likely to succeed.
It will be a further step towards full sovereignty, another step added to those taken in the same direction by Liberal administrations, for instance the signing of our own treaties, the ending of appeals to the privy council, the disappearance of the word dominion, and the appointment of the first Canadian governor general.
Before I bring my speech to a close, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about another project put forward by the Montreal newspaper La Presse. I am thinking of the organization of a universal exhibition in Canada in 1967. That newspaper recently published a series of very interesting articles on the matter by Laurent Lauzier.
Last April the Montreal committee of the Canadian universal exhibition submitted to federal and provincial authorities and to the city of Montreal a report urging the organization of a universal exhibition in 1967 in the Canadian metropolis for the centennial of confederation.
The project no doubt should be taken into favourable consideration by the government.
Besides the circumstance of the date, the whole world's attention is focused on Canada on account of its influence in the economic and political fields. In the field of culture, particularly since the Canada Council was established in 1957, our country is progressing rapidly toward real maturity.

With its picturesque and varied scenery, its natural resources and the diversity of its people, Canada has everything to offer as the scene of a world exhibition.
On the other hand, Montreal, metropolis of the country, second largest French city in the world, with its location, its industrial development, its commercial activity, its port, its railway and air terminals, the St. Lawrence seaway, its cosmopolitan aspect and international atmosphere, leads all other Canadian cities as a site for such an exhibition.
I realize that we are still seven years away from 1967.
However, it is not premature to consider the project seriously, nor too early for the Canadian authorities to submit a request in the matter to the International Bureau of Exhibitions in Paris. Indeed a project such as this calls for years of preparation.
I am, of course, in favour of the project and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is responsible for such action, will perhaps be kind enough to make a few comments on the subject in due time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to add my congratulations to those which have already been extended to the mover (Mr. Morissette) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne for his expert address on the economy of the country; and to the very gracious hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman) for her real contribution to this debate.
From some of the opposition benches we have heard a great deal about the emptiness of this speech from the throne. I would merely suggest, Mr. Speaker, that in that speech from the throne there are many things which the ordinary people in this country will appreciate and to which they are looking forward. Certainly we note with pleasure the government's announcement that amendments to the Old Age Security Act and the War Veterans Allowance Act will be placed before parliament to make these pensions payable outside of Canada. We commend the government for this action; we think it is a generous and just gesture to the elderly citizens of our country.
I should also like to urge that the idea of a physical fitness council be accepted for the improvement of our physical health. I should like to add that I feel they should also accept the responsibility for mental health, and that a combined council to encourage physical and mental health could do a great deal for the health of this country. Certainly physical health is important,
The Address-Mr. H. M. Horner but the ability of our people to think clearly and logically is perhaps more important than the physical aspect.
The people in my constituency will be pleased to find in the speech from the throne the announcement that a new department of forestry will be set up. Inasmuch as a great deal of the forest industry in Alberta is concentrated in my riding we look forward to this department providing a lead, in co-operation with the provinces in the development of our forest industries. With the only pulp mill in the prairie provinces located at Hinton in my riding, this is a matter of major concern to us. With major lumber industries in the Edson and White-court areas we would urge the government to continue its program of research into the use of lodgepole pine as material for the pulp and paper industry. And we might suggest to the government that the locale of Edson might make an excellent site for any future forest research laboratory. One other suggestion with regard to this new department of forestry which I should like to make is that perhaps we should give consideration to placing the national parks under this new department, as they are certainly related resources.
Now I should like to turn to agriculture for a few moments. It would seem to me that agriculture in Canada is now at the crossroads. Which way will it go; to the large integrated companies, as suggested by one of the eastern daily papers, or to the well integrated, well managed, properly capitalized family farms? There is no doubt in my mind that the family farm is the best and most economical producer, and that it should be encouraged and helped.
It might be well at this time to place the rest of the house on record with regard to this question. Right now I gather from what the opposition say that they would rather see integration and corporate farming. The C.C.F. seem to vacillate between the two, and would appear to put more emphasis on large corporate farming. Certainly there has never been any doubt so far as the policy of this government is concerned. Our stand has been clear; to help the family farm and its operations.
We have heard a considerable amount about agriculture in this debate, some of it from hon. members opposite most uninformed with regard to the facts. What are the facts with respect to agriculture, particularly as they pertain to western agriculture? The first is that we can produce in Canada at least twice as much food as we do now. We have done this before in times of stress, and we can do it again as soon as there are markets available to absorb our production. If we

The Address-Mr. H. M. Horner were to pile up produce at government expense only to have it spoil or see it destroyed, that would be a waste which could not be excused. Only a portion of our surplus can be assimilated by overseas and local welfare agencies even on a giveaway basis. Incentive support programs will pile up unmanageable surpluses, as has been conclusively shown by the results of the United States program and by some programs here in Canada. We are a high cost economy, yet we depend on exports for our prosperity. Therefore our produce must be priced in relation to world markets.
Because of the contribution which farmers made during the war, because of tariff protection of industry, because of a high cost of production over which agriculture has no control, the government of Canada has a moral and legal obligation to the farmers of this country. The Stewart commission has shown that the corporations have failed in their efforts to do a good job in the pricing and distribution of products to the consumer, primarily because of their desire for profits which are higher than normal. We are convinced that these same corporations should not have control over the production of our foodstuffs. We are equally convinced that the most economical producer is the family farmer-the man who has certainly been vindicated by the Stewart commission in this regard. He must have support if he is to survive, and I am proud to say that he has the support of this government.
One of the major reasons why corporate farming cannot be as efficient as individual family farms is the fact that with family farms we have individual management and very little of the top-heavy overhead which is bogging down so many corporations at the present time and diminishing the production of goods and services in Canada. The announced intention of the stabilization act was to maintain prices, using a flexible program to provide markets, support the family farm and prevent the accumulation of unmanageable surpluses. This is one reason we have used deficiency payments in respect to a number of products in the past. These deficiency payment programs have worked well as applied to wool, apples and other products.
The announced intention of the government to use a deficiency payment program with regard to eggs and hogs was made early last year. I am sure this program can work in respect to both these commodities if it is given a chance by the producers, a chance by members of parliament and, most important of all, by the trade concerned with each product. If the trade will not co-operate, then marketing boards on a national level become an absolute necessity.

As an example, let us consider the situation with regard to eggs. Under the former system of support, with government purchase at a floor price level, the support was given to the produce buyer and the packer. In effect, they had a daily floor price. All their storage stocks became government stocks for which the government paid them. Then the government started to pay storage. The effect was to give these people free inventory and free cold storage plants. It also gave them an incentive to become producers to complete the cycle of a government-guaranteed business.
Opponents of the present plan suggest that the government should have reduced the support, and say this would have accomplished the same thing. Not at all. The reduction of the support price would have killed the family farm and handed production over to large integrated units which would then have had control and been able to push up prices at will. The other disadvantage of government purchase was that people concerned with the trade would never venture into export markets because they were never obliged to. They left that to the government, and sold all their excess to the government.
The principle of deficiency payments in this field is an absolute necessity if we are going to support the family farm, and if we intend to have a healthy, independent, agricultural economy. The mechanics of this program will have to be worked out. There are bound to be some wrinkles. We expect that, and look forward to trying to help make this plan work.
It has also become apparent with regard to eggs that the trade has done everything possible to influence the farmer to dislike this plan, because it takes the trade off the gravy train. One look at the price spread between one province and another will convince one that there is some manipulation of prices going on. Certainly it does not cost 12 to 18 cents to ship a dozen eggs from Alberta to Ontario, yet this has been the spread at various times over the past few months. Now the spread is down to 4 and 5 cents between Alberta and Ontario, and this is the way it should be. This proves how wrong the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulangerj was when he said, as reported at page 25 of Hansard, that western farmers would be the hardest hit by this legislation in view of the price gap in relation to other parts of the country.
I would point out to the hon. member that on a national average we in western Canada will gain a little from that price spread, as the Minister of Agriculture stated yesterday.
It becomes apparent that in Canada there is a virtual monopoly in the egg business.

This new scheme is bothering the trade, and they are doing everything possible to try to convince the producer that it is not a good idea, all of which is more evidence than should be required to promote the idea of producer marketing boards across Canada. I realize that the federal government has no jurisdiction over the provincial sale of eggs, but I feel that consideration should be given to allowing the stabilization board to have control of interprovincial shipments and to encouraging the provinces to set up marketing boards using the stabilization board as a national co-ordinating facility.
It was quite wrong when the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) stated that we did not discuss this program. Of course we did. I spent most of the summer discussing the program with farmers throughout my constituency, and I have yet to hear one say that the old program was better. They are willing to accept this program. We have to get behind it and show them it can work. It is not in the best interests of the country for people who know nothing about the program and who do not understand it to stand up in this house and call it down, as some have done.
I should like to say a word with regard to the sheep industry in Canada. I would urge the minister to give serious and favourable consideration to the report and recommendations which were brought in by the sheep committee in the latter part of 1959. Further to their recommendations, I believe that a standardized system of carcass grading is absolutely essential to the prosperity of our sheep industry and should be considered along with the other recommendations in this regard.
From time to time, as legislation is brought before this house on matters which have had particular reference to western Canada, we have heard a great deal of noise from the opposition benches in regard to what they would like for areas from which they come. We heard on one occasion last year, during discussion of a western farm bill, a dissertation on codfish. This year we have heard dissertations on soybeans and other things in eastern Canada. I can assure the house that we in western Canada realize and are willing to work on problems of other areas, but we do have regional problems that can only be settled in a regional way. We feel it is a matter of disrespect to western Canada for these hon. members to continue to act as they have in the last year or two each time western legislation has been before the house.
Further to that, on occasion there has been some confusion as to what we do want
The Address-Mr. H. M. Horner
for agriculture in western Canada, and perhaps for the benefit of the house and the government I could briefly summarize what we desire. First of all, we want prices for our produce which bear a true relationship to costs, bearing in mind efficiency improvements due to technical changes. Second, we want stability of those prices so we can plan our future with some degree of success. Third, we would like as free access to the markets of the world as is feasible, and we do not mean by paying lip service to the free trade idea of the Liberal party.
We have witnessed a very strange spectacle in the last few days. Hon. gentlemen opposite have been talking about free trade. Mention was made of some cars coming in from Russia. Who was the first hon. member to get up and object? It was the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). We have also heard a lot about textiles in the last few days and the need for more protection for that industry. Who have been bringing forward all these things? The free trade experts. As I say, it is time we had a little realistic thinking about trade on the part of the Liberal party.
We would also like to see more people in Canada, because more immigration increases our own domestic markets for our products.
We would like to see more responsibility in marketing by the people in the trade. We commend the government and the Minister of Trade and Commerce for what he has done from the government side particularly in marketing our grains.
We want to see more responsibility in the field of storage, and more responsibility assumed by those people who are concerned with distributing the goods we produce to the consumer, and here we refer these people to the Stewart commission. The only available solution here is the producer marketing board.
We want to see continued government research in marketing and production. We want to see continued government control and research in the field of animal and plant diseases. Certainly we can commend the minister and his department in this regard. We commend the government, too, for the crop assistance scheme introduced in the last session of parliament. This is an absolute necessity for farmers in western Canada. It may take a few years for this plan to shake down into a generally usable scheme, but it had to be started and we are proud that the government to which we belong started it.
We are also appreciative of what the government has done in regard to farm credit, in spite of those in western Canada who complain that it does not do any good
628	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. H. M. Horner to give further credit to already debt-ridden farmers. It is an irrefutable fact that if the family farm is going to continue as an efficient producing unit it is going to have to be properly capitalized.
We would also like to see the prices of some of the things we buy, and particularly farm machinery, cars and trucks, brought more into line with the prices we receive. We can see no value in having the farmers of western Canada pay for the style changes and retooling that are required every year or two because our Canadian manufacturers are trying to keep up with their United States counterparts. If this trend by Canadian manufacturers continues they will find that they will start to lose an increasing volume to imported farm machinery, because our farmers are just not going to pay the costs as they have done in the past.
These are some of the things we require for western Canadian agriculture. I consider all of them basic. This government in two and one half years has instituted more of them than any other government in Canada in any previous 20-year period. We urge the government to consider those things which are yet to be done, and to implement them as soon as possible.
With respect to rapeseed I should like to support the admirable work done by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Rapp) in asking to have rapeseed classified as a grain. Here I would ask the government to take into consideration the recommendations made last year by the committee on agriculture and colonization.
Another regional problem we have in the northern part of the prairies, and particularly in those areas not now covered by the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, concerns conservation. We would urge the government to give consideration to extending this act to the northern part of the prairies. We are concerned that conservation measures be instituted here in such a manner as to conserve our soil and water and assist in flood control measures.
In my constituency we have a voluntary organization known as the Pembina river conservation and drainage association which has done much work in this regard along the Pembina river. Assistance under the P.F.R.A. would assist them in their work and enhance the cause of conservation.
We are happy to hear that plans for a national conservation conference are continuing. This must be the first big step before any effective land use program can be instituted. My constituents are conservation conscious, and are watching these developments with interest.


Before I conclude may I say that in 195758 the people of this country made a decision that they would like to see some changes in the way things were run. I suggest that these changes have been made with foresight and vigour and that when these changes were made those people most affected by them reacted to the greatest degree. If a government is going to be firm and continue to govern in a wise manner, then it cannot give in to every pressure group in the country. I suggest it is not fitting that some of the questions that have been brought up by pressure groups should be forced upon the government in any way at all. The decisions confronting the government are for the government to make. We are proud of the way it is making its decisions, and will continue to support the government in its important work.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to address this obviously enthusiastic audience I must first of all congratulate the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Morissette) and the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman) as mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the maiden speech of the hon. member for Grenville-Dundas was a delightful parliamentary manifestation of earnestness, equipoise and euphony.
Now, Mr. Speaker, before launching on to my main topic, because I am somewhat optimistic by nature, I think we in this House of Commons should as Canadians, all of us, have a sense of gratitude for the opportunity to live in this beautiful land, so rich in resources and so abundantly provided with opportunities for people and for governments. I am confident, Mr. Speaker, that if we only use our intelligence and our industry and apply them to our human and natural resources we can solve our problems in the Canadian and democratic way.
I think we should also be grateful that we live in a land of democratic institutions, as reflected in this parliament, with all its failings. It is a human institution, a reflection of the people in this country. We should not forget, in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that half the world has copied this type of institution at this time, and a great section of the world is trying to produce or reproduce the pattern established by the mother of parliaments at Westminster in Great Britain. As I see it, Mr. Speaker, a true democracy is a society in which there is healthy conflict within a framework of effective, legitimate government, recognized by all parties to that conflict. This is represented, I suppose, to the best advantage in the world today in the

parliament at Westminster, where the lusty debates on policies are tempered with wit and fertilized with humour.
In concluding my remarks is this fashion I wish to emphasize that "Made in Britain" still is a mighty good brand for all freedom seeking and freedom loving people to patronize.
I intended to speak on several questions which are raised in the speech from the throne. In fact I have in my office now laid aside a masterpiece from experience. Owing to certain local developments and the importance of and my interest in a very current problem, I shall deal largely with the development of the Columbia river basin in Canada. However, I cannot resist the opportunity at this time to welcome the decision of the government to establish a department of forests; for this recognition is an important thing to Canada, in my opinion possibly much more important than many people would realize at this time; important to the people themselves, important to the government, and I am sure that in days to come it will be mighty important to the treasury of this country. This step has been urged for years by a number of organizations across this country and by a number of members in this house including, in all modesty, Mr. Speaker, the member for Kootenay West. I shall have more to say on this question when the bill to give effect to this step comes before the house.
The mention of amendments to the Old Age Security Act and the War Veterans Allowance Act to provide for payment of pensions and allowances outside of Canada is all to the good. It has been urged' by members of all parties in this house on different occasions. However, we in this-I was going to say "group", Mr. Speaker, but it is getting to be such a common word in this house that I think it better to say "this band of happy warriors"-we in this band of happy warriors regret there is no mention of any increase in old age security payments, or of an amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act to increase the allowable income of recipients. I am sure many war disability pensioners will be disappointed that there is no provision for an increase in war disability pensions. We will have more to say on that at a later date as well.
Other members of this happy band, my colleagues, already in this debate have dealt effectively with the problems concerning fiscal policies, defence, trade, markets, housing, unemployment, civil service salaries. Because of the limitations of time and' my anxiety to deal with a particular question I am not going to deal with those questions now.
Question of Privilege
However, before launching myself on to the Columbia I do wish to express my support for the concern of the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl), over recent manifestations in the world and in Canada resulting from the scourge of the swastika. I have personal knowledge of a number of individual expressions of admiration for that philosophy, but time does not permit me to tell the house now. It is a thing I hate, Mr. Speaker. This is a virus that can be very insidious.
However, while I fully understand and appreciate the hon. member's desire for the government to take legislative action as a deterrent to those insidious hatemongers, I cannot agree that this would be an effective remedy. I think it safe to say, Mr. Speaker, that history proves it is almost impossible to successfully legislate against the intangible delinquencies of mankind. In my opinion it is the duty of all Canadians to extinguish these sparks of intolerance by their influence and demonstrations of their faith in democratic principles. Before leaving this question I suggest also that it would be a good thing, an excellent idea in fact, if such books as The Diary of Anne Frank and The Scourge of the Swastika by Lord Russell were made required reading in all high schools in this country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, having reached the Columbia river in my progress and in my oration, may I suggest that you call it one o'clock.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned for some bodily sustenance at one o'clock I had just reached the banks of the Columbia river. I wish to deal particularly with a paragraph in the throne speech that is of prime importance to the people of Canada and of great interest to the people of British Columbia generally and to the people of the Kootenays in particular. I quote from page 2 of Hansard this paragraph in the throne speech:
Substantial progress has now been made in finding a satisfactory basis for the development of the power of the Columbia river in co-operation with

the United States and negotiations for this purpose have now been initiated with the government of the United States. The results will be placed before parliament for approval and for the authority to take the measures necessary to bring about the full use of this most valuable source of power. The government of Canada remains ready to participate with British Columbia in the joint development of the potentials of this great river.
In dealing with this question, Mr. Speaker, we must realize that the Columbia is to power production what the Mississippi is to navigation or the Nile to irrigation. It is one of the great rivers of North America, exceeded only by the Mississippi and the St. Lawrence in the amount of water it discharges annually into the ocean. Its total length is 1,210 miles, of which 465 are in Canada. It has a total fall of 2,650 feet from its headwaters to the sea and 1,360 feet of this fall are in Canada, which shows the great advantage of storage in Canada. The Columbia river basin has an area of 259,000 square miles, of which 39,700 are in Canada.
It is estimated that there can be developed a total installed capacity of 35 million kilowatts with over 4 million of this total in Canada. This represents 30 per cent of the total water power potential of Canada and the United States combined. In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I wish to quote from the report of a committee of congress on the Columbia river which was appointed in 1943 to study the possibility of developing the United States portion of the Columbia river basin. The report had this to say in part:
From the standpoint of resources the Columbia is the mightiest stream on the North American continent, its potential almost beyond comprehension, for nature in one of her philanthropic moods fashioned the land with such perfection as is nowhere else known.
I mention the few facts, Mr. Speaker, to bring into focus and to create a proper conception of the magnitude of the resources that are being dealt with according to this paragraph in the throne speech. The investigation of the resources of the Columbia, as many members will recall, is the result of a reference to the international joint commission which was tabled in this house and in Washington on March 9, 1944. On February 21 and 22, 1949 in this house I presented the C.C.F. policy with respect to the development of the Columbia basin in Canada.
I might say at this time that we are very glad to see that the government of Canada is following along the lines of the policy that we suggested then. In fairness I must also say, Mr. Speaker, that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) also took a very similar approach at that time and has continued to maintain the same approach since

he attained his high office. As found on page 775 of Hansard for February 22, 1949 I said:
-consideration should be given by this government to the development of the water resources in the basin under public ownership in co-operation with the government of British Columbia. I am recommending the establishment of a Canadian Columbia river basin authority, and in support of that proposal I should like to quote from the minutes of a committee of congress which sat in 1933-34 to consider this question and which reported with respect to the United States portion of the Columbia river basin as follows:
"We believe in private enterprise-in the expectancy of rewards for honest endeavour, labour, initiative and daring"-
