And so do we. I continue:
"-in the things that have made America great. But some things are too big for private enterprise, and the Columbia river is one of these."
I also made this suggestion:
-the Columbia river basin is rich in history and rich in possibilities for the taking of an excellent documentary film by the national film board- I think that the national film board could make a great contribution towards arousing the interest of the youth of our country by undertaking a documentary film covering the development of the Columbia river basin.
I am very glad to know that provision has been made by the government for the making of a documentary film of the Columbia river basin. I said the minister had the same approach, and I congratulate him for his consistency after taking office. If I am allowed a play on words, Mr. Speaker, the minister knows very well how "Green" is our valley.
Now, Mr. Speaker, some years ago the former government took this matter out of the hands of the international joint commission and carried on discussions at the high political level, I think with the idea of speeding things up. However, those discussions were on the whole fruitless, and progress toward an agreement between Canada and the United States was almost nil. After 15 years of engineering studies by the international Columbia river engineering board, they presented their report to the international joint commission early last year, after the Canadian government had spent approximately $5 million since 1945 on surveys and research to obtain the essential information.
Then in identical letters to the United States and Canadian sections of the international joint commission dated January 8, 1959 and January 29, 1959 respectively, the secretary of state of the United States and the Secretary of State for External Affairs for Canada referred to the general objectives of the Columbia reference of March, 1944 and requested from the international joint commission a special report, as follows:
The Address-Mr. Herridge
The governments of the United States and Canada, as a part of their continuing discussions, have agreed to request the international joint commission to report specially to the governments at an early date its recommendations concerning the principles to be applied in determining:
(a)	the benefits which will result from the co-operative use of storage of waters and electrical interconnection within the Columbia river system; and
(b)	the apportionment between the two countries of such benefits more particularly in regard to electrical generation and flood control.
I want to say at this time, Mr. Speaker, that we were very pleased indeed when we saw the government return, shall I say, the technical aspects of the discussion on this important question to the international joint commission. This action on their part has been fully justified by the speed with which negotiations have been carried on and accelerated, and the result shown by the report of the international joint commission. This report of the international joint commission of the United States and Canada as proposed for determining and apportioning benefit from the co-operative use and storage of water and electrical interconnections within the Columbia river system was made public a few days ago. I may say it is a most interesting and possibly a unique document. So far as I can find out it is the only document of its kind in Canadian history dealing with a problem of this type.
On Monday, January 25 the Prime Minister announced that negotiations between Canada and the United States for the development of the water resources of the Columbia river system are to commence in Ottawa on Thursday, February 11. Step by step we seem to be making some headway. He announced also that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) would be the chairman of the Canadian delegation, the other members being Mr. Robertson, deputy minister of northern affairs and national resources, Mr. A. E. Ritchie, assistant undersecretary, Department of External Affairs, and Mr. E. W. Bassett, deputy minister of lands and forests of the province of British Columbia.
I should like to compliment the Secretary of State for External Affairs, on behalf of this band of warriors, as I said before, for the vigorous way in which he has handled this question and for the soundness of the procedures adopted. His actions and efforts are the subject of general satisfaction in British Columbia, and in particular in the Kootenays and that portion of the Kootenays which I have the honour to represent.
I also wish to express the appreciation of my constituents for the great work done by General McNaughton for Canada throughout the years. Both in Canada and in the United States his devotion to the principles of equity

The Address

Mr. Herridge and fair play for all governments and peoples concerned is generally recognized. He does not seek to get the best of anyone. He has sought to get this problem settled on the basis of justice and equity to all the governments and peoples concerned. Editorials in a number of United States newspapers and journals also contain flattering testimonials to General McNaughton. I want to quote from the Engineering News Record of November 12, 1959 at page 116. Under the heading "Choose Right Man for IJC", I read this:
United States representation on the international joint commission has been without a permanent head since the death of Douglas McKay, former interior secretary, last July.
It is appropriate to note here that Canada's three-man half of I.J.C. is headed by an engineer and administrator of great prestige, vigour and ability-A.G.L. McNaughton. General McNaughton represents Canada's interests in the I.J.C. with unquestionable competence.
In the best interests of our nation, President Eisenhower should name a worthy counterpart for General McNaughton-and fairly soon.
In that connection I want to pay tribute to his loyal colleagues on the commission and their loyal staff. Very seldom have I witnessed a staff serving a commission which enters into the spirit and purpose of the commission more than does the staff of the international joint commission.
I was glad to note, Mr. Speaker, the recent co-operation between the federal and provincial governments, something to which we have looked forward, on this important issue and Premier Bennett's recent announcement that both governments now agree on a national position with respect to this development.
During the period of these negotiations we have had a lot of propaganda from the Peace River Development Company. Mr. Main-waring says that the Peace river power can be developed in eight years, and that it will take 13 years to develop power on the Columbia river. However, I am reliably informed that power from the Columbia river can be provided in 6J years by the building of the Mica creek dam.
Mr. Mainwaring accuses the federal government of false optimism. I am glad we have some people in the federal government handling this question who are optimistic and capable of getting the ball rolling. I think in all these statements Mr. Mainwaring is trying to throw cold water on the development of the water resources of the Columbia under a public authority. No doubt we will need all our water resources in British Columbia developed, but it is a matter of timing and economics. I think anyone who studies the evidence will realize that this evidence clearly proves it is in the public interest that the Columbia be developed first.

Without any doubt there is overwhelming public support in British Columbia for the development of the Columbia first, and under a public authority, as has been demonstrated by a resolution of the British Columbia chamber of commerce, I think in 1957, urging the development of Mica creek and that it be entrusted to the British Columbia power commission; resolutions of Kootenay chambers of commerce, municipalities and other organizations; and a public opinion poll conducted by the Sun of Vancouver on August 24, 1957.
At this point I want to compliment the Sun Publishing Company for issuing a very excellent brochure on electric power in British Columbia. In doing this they have performed a public service by bringing together in one easily read document a good many of the facts concerning this important development. The public opinion poll showed that 69 per cent were in favour of public ownership and only 11 per cent in favour of private ownership. There were 4 per cent who did not seem to care, but in any society that is the normal percentage who do not seem to care.
Then there is another report that I had very recently concerning the experience of the people in the United States. This report had a history of the success achieved in producing low cost power by the Tennessee valley authority, by the Ontario hydro commission, by Winnipeg hydro and at Bonneville and Grand Coulee. The cheapest power in the world is developed at Bonneville and Grand Coulee under a public authority.
There is unanimous support for the building of the Mica creek dam as the first project. In my constituency there is unanimous support for the building of a dam on Murphy creek, known as Low Arrow. However, Mr. Speaker, the people of Kootenay West are concerned over proposals to build what is known as the High Arrow dam north of Castlegar. This dam would raise the lake level 44 feet above normal high water, and seriously flood and affect the district north as far as Revelstoke. It would flood or partially flood 18 communities covering over 40,000 acres of good land, and it would mean the displacement at the present time of some 1600 or more now and prevent the settlement of thousands more in the days to come. It would destroy industrial sites, flood our beaches, render useless wharf facilities, make an almost impossible condition with respect to the booming of logs and the dumping of logs in rivers and leave us, shall I say, with this great draw-down from high water to low water, and thus leave great waste and desolation throughout a good portion of the area, separate communities on one side of

the lake from those on the other. There would not be a kilowatt of power produced in Canada from this dam.
There is strong opposition to this proposal, as indicated by the papers recently. For example, the Nelson Daily News which I have says "dam draws fire". I have heard from the Castlegar and district chamber of commerce, the Nakusp chamber of commerce and the associated chambers of commerce and individuals from Rossland to Revelstoke.
What are we asked to sacrifice all this great land for? We are asked to sacrifice for certain downstream benefits when it is obvious, from the change in the development of power in the United States, the turnover from thermo power to firm power, that we may receive these benefits for only from 25 to 30 years.
The residents of the Columbia river basin do not intend to be silent spectators in the coming drama of development, but understanding and active members of the cast, playing their parts with purpose and in harmony to the benefit of all and to the benefit of Canada. The West Kootenay rod and gun club association has made certain proposals with respect to a biological survey of the basin to determine the effect on game and fisheries of the Columbia and Kootenay river developments and compensation to correct certain things caused by the building of dams and so on. Our people take a great interest in this question.
Before passing on I just want to refer to a statement made by Mr. McMynn, a senior official of the West Kootenay Light and Power Company Limited, as reported in the Trail Daily Times of January 25, 1960. He is reported as follows:
Mr. McMynn declared that a lot of Arrow lakes property was "continually bothered" with flooding now, without any development on the Arrow lakes at all. "It occurred to us." he said, "that if the owners of that property could be relocated satisfactorily above high water, and the cost of relocation were paid by the authority making the development, then a great number of people inhabiting the Arrow lakes would be pleased to see that happen."
Yet at the same time, while Mr. McMynn talks of no development, other people talk of the compensation required as about $30 million. Mr. McMynn is a very likeable person, but all I can say in response to that statement is that he must have had a touch of gout the evening before he made a statement like that, because he could not have been considering the question in a broad, objective way.
I have mentioned the protests that have been made, Mr. Speaker. In conclusion I want to emphasize a few facts. This is a matter that must be given consideration. We are opposed to flooding this beautiful valley
The Address-Mr. Herridge for the damming of water without any power being produced in Canada, with the desolation which will result, and also for relatively short run benefits. We believe we have a responsibility to future generations.
The people I represent are a concerned people. At the present time chambers of commerce, rod and gun clubs, church groups and other organizations are really studying this matter seriously because they feel they are participants in this matter, and rightly so, as Canadians. I mention their fears to the house and to the minister at this time. However, while these fears are justified, I suggest that we must get together on the things upon which we can agree.
In conclusion I must emphasize the fact that in British Columbia there is unanimous support for the public development of the Columbia river basin waters. There is unanimous support for dominion-provincial co-operation in this development. There is the Mica creek dam. There is unanimous support for the building of the Murphy creek dam or in other words the Low Arrow dam. I suggest that we must take a positive approach, and must not let our fears with respect to sectional interests take our eyes, shall I say, off the dream, as it were, of the major development. Therefore we must work together on these major proposals in a positive way.
I therefore suggest that every effort be made to secure agreement on a treaty and reach a successful conclusion with respect to these problems by establishing the principles for the division of downstream benefits outlined in the document tabled recently by the Prime Minister, by agreement for the co-operation of the provincial and dominion governments for the first building of Mica creek dam, and from that point continuing negotiations between representatives of Canada and representatives of the United States for the settlement of those other outstanding problems.
I am one who is rather hesitant to plunge into things too quickly. As time passes things are brought into proper focus and perspective. If we can get a treaty on the things I have mentioned, we can then continue studies and negotiations for the settlement of these outstanding problems over a period of years. If we start on Mica creek we will have made a great start in the right direction. We will have indicated to the rest of Canada that public ownership is going to be a dominant influence in the development and distribution of power in British Columbia. We would realize that we are seizing and dealing with an important question step by step and in a logical manner.

The Address-Mr. Crouse
I make these proposals to the minister. I believe that if we enter this thing in the right spirit, both in British Columbia, in the communities directly affected, and as Canada in dealing with our neighbours across the line, we shall finally come to a solution which is satisfactory to all without the desecration of any natural resources.
Therefore in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say this. I am sure that our negotiating team which commences its negotiations with its opposite numbers in the United States on February 11, undertakes its duties and its responsibilities with the best wishes of all members of this house, in high hopes that their labours will be crowned with success and that with the application of intelligence, industry and co-operation on the part of everyone concerned, the people of Canada and the people of the United States will benefit from this great development now and in the days to come.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the member of parliament from the historic riding of Queens-Lunenberg I am pleased to have this opportunity to participate in this debate. My first words will be to you, to express my satisfaction at seeing you again in the chair in evident good health after your recent strenuous travels. I would also like to join with those who have preceded me in extending my best wishes to the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn) upon his elevation to the position of Deputy Speaker. It is an appointment that has met with the approval of hon. members on 'both sides of this house, and I wish him every success in his new position.
Congratulations are also extended to the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Morissette) as well as to the hon. and gracious member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman), not only for the splendid addresses they made but also for the honour that was granted to them in being selected to move and second the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
Traditionally, the speech from the throne sets forth the intent of the government of the day with respect to its actions in the ensuing parliament, and describes what it proposes to do for the people of this country. The speech from the throne which we heard read at the opening of this session was exceptional in that the words showed a positive understanding of the problems of the Canadian people and indicated that effective steps would be taken to meet these problems. I believe the Prime Minister and his cabinet deserve the commendation of every Canadian for their careful planning of this program. The government is doing for the people of this country the very best it is possible to do at this time.
[Mr. Herridge.l

However, there has been all kinds of criticism from the opposition benches, most of it quite lengthy but none, as far as I can determine, of a type that could be considered constructive. When the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) spoke, most of his criticisms of our policies were a rebroadcast so far as I am concerned, for he said the same things when he honoured me by visiting my constituency and spoke at Bridgewater on my birthday, November 19. At that time, however, he said that in 1957 Canada was enjoying a boom, while now we have the highest interest rates, inflation, and tightest money in our history.
I might say from the comments received that this type of speech made little impression on the good people of Queens-Lunenburg, but it did leave them with the feeling the Leader of the Opposition, or his party, could not do anything better than is being done. In fact in my opinion, which is shared by many, a great deal of the criticism is woefully weak; and although hon. gentlemen opposite have spoken at great length on a variety of topics, important constructive matters have been barely mentioned.
The negative policies of the Liberal party today have made little or no impression on the people of Canada, and the riding of Queens-Lunenburg is no exception. The reason behind this is readily understood when one reads the history of the people of my constituency. The early settlers came to Lunenburg county in 1753 from the Rhenish palatinate in Hanover. They suffered untold hardship and severe difficulties. However, they persevered, and today my constituents are divided roughly into two groups; those associated with agriculture and forestry and those who make their living on the sea and in allied industries.
The amazing fact about these early settlers is that they come to Nova Scotia to become farmers, but through necessity at least one half of these inland peasants took to the sea and became known as the best sailors and fishermen on the north Atlantic. The skills, the methods and the experience they gained have been passed down through the years, and today the citizens of my riding are well known for their thrift, their ambition, and their willingness to work.
When the Leader of the Opposition spoke of high interest rates in my riding he was apparently unaware of the background of this constituency, and the fact that my thrifty constituents prefer investing their hard earned savings at a satisfactory rate of interest. His criticism of so-called tight money also fell upon deaf ears, for my constituents have long been known as prudent people.

They welcome economic conservatism, a tightening of the reins on money, a stringent policy of budget balancing and curtailment of unnecessary government spending. This is true because generally speaking they are tough bargainers who pay as they go, who can and will use the resources at hand, and are against deficit spending.
When the Leader of the Opposition spoke of inflation he made no impression on the people of Queens-Lunenburg, for they know we cannot have steeply rising government expenditures, rapid economic expansion, easy money and a stable dollar, all at the same time. We have to make a choice. If we want more capital and credit for private industry we should not expect as a nation to place ever-mounting responsibilities on the federal and provincial governments. It is an evident fact in any economy that the capital and credit taken by the government is not available for anyone else.
Today there is a persistent tendency by many people to divert more and more productive resources into the hands of government. These people look upon federal government bodies as all-powerful forces capable of supplying their every need and shouldering all their responsibilities. I believe it is opportune to examine this dangerous trend toward dependence on the federal government, and point out to Canadians generally that the path to true progress in this nation does not lie in more government control and increased welfare plans but in a free competitive private enterprise system which is a living symbol not only of opportunity, but also of plenty, of human dignity, and of security for all Canadians.
We must speak out more forcefully in support of the capitalist system. It is capitalism's system of competition, and of freedom to profit through service to the consumer, which produces the goods. The apostles of socialism and of communism in this country, if not blinded by party zeal, cannot help but realize that anything communism or socialism can do, capitalism is already doing better. I believe the free enterprise system has proved itself to be the only system that enables man to preserve his individual liberties while at the same time providing him with the maximum opportunity to improve his living conditions. The standards of living enjoyed by the vast majority of people in North America are the clearest evidence of this truth.
When speaking of inflation we must also realize that there is no fixed value to the Canadian dollar. It floats freely on the Canadian economy, as freely as an abandoned ship on the ocean. We know that today the dollar
The Address-Mr. Crouse will only buy approximately half what it could buy 15 years ago, and we call this inflation. Newspaper editorials loudly call for action on this inflationary trend. They are all calling on somebody to do something, and invariably they ask, "Why doesn't the government do something?"
The truth of the matter is that the answer does not lie with the government but with the Canadian people. No government in a democratic country like Canada can control, or wishes to control, the minds of the people. As Canadians and as individuals we have certain freedoms. We are free to worship as we please, free to choose our own occupation, and work when it pleases us, although this freedom is gradually being taken away; free to elect the government of our choice, and free to set the value of our currency. Yes; this too is one of our freedoms. We, individually and collectively, set the value of our floating Canadian dollar; the government can only print the paper and mint the coins.
The decision as to the amount this paper and coinage is worth rests upon your shoulders, and from the creeping inflation experienced in Canada since 1939 it would appear that many are no longer interested in the value of a dollar but only in the quantity of dollars secured. By demanding more pay per hour without increasing production; by demanding less work hours per week without decreasing fixed company costs like insurance, taxes and yearly maintenance costs, and by seeking higher corporate profits, our unit costs have increased until we are no longer competitive in world markets nor in some of our Canadian markets. This loss of sales in competitive markets has caused some factories to close, with resulting unemployment which requires make-work programs that further increase taxes on the remaining producing companies.
In Nova Scotia and in the Atlantic area generally our fishermen have long known that increased earnings or wealth can come only from increased production and sales. I believe the adoption of this principle on a national basis is the only effective curb on inflation. Combine this with governmental economy so that we can live within our income, and Canadians will enjoy the greatest national growth and peace of mind ever experienced in their history.
I was somewhat amazed at the remarks made on January 22 by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier). This self-styled democratic socialist, who is not of the inner six or the outer seven but one of the divided eight, stated that there is no use
636	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Crouse in organized labour electing a capitalist government, that this would be ridiculous. In saying that, the hon. gentleman who belongs, as the former speaker said, to a happy band- a band which in my opinion plays a discordant note on eight different kinds of ideology- completely ignored the fact that most of the workers in Canada today, whether unionists or not, own stock either directly in Canadian companies or indirectly through insurance policies. These men may not be large capitalists; nevertheless they are capitalists, and it was these workers who elected a Conservative government to this house in 1957 and again in 1958.
The hon. member showed a further lack of knowledge regarding monetary matters when he suggested the establishment of a national investment board that would issue bonds and make capital available at an interest rate of not more than 3 per cent. He further stated that this board would compel the implementation of its recommendations, which is an action, I believe, foreign to our freedom loving democratic people and which gives an indication of the bureaucratic control Canadians would suffer if ever-heaven forbid- a socialist government were elected in Ottawa.
In the speech from the throne there is an important paragraph which reads as follows:
We are heartened by the unanimous approval given by the United Nations to the Canadian proposal to sample and analyse more widely and effectively the radioactive content of the atmosphere, soil and food. For this purpose necessary funds to enable Canada to take a leading part in this work will be requested.
The importance of this section of the throne speech cannot be overemphasized, especially when consideration is given to the danger to those yet unborn from radioactive substances. However, this section mentions an analysis only of the atmosphere, soil and food. In view of the productivity of our fisheries I would suggest to the government that an analysis of the water in the ocean, and in the rivers and lakes, be also maintained. I wonder how many people are aware of the fact that the atomic energy commission of the United States has an ocean dump site for radioactive waste material only 12 miles from Boston. The atomic energy commission has been using this dump site for the past 13 years to dispose of materials that are low in radioactivity and generally consist of residual solutions from experiments, contaminated paper, cloth, glassware and equipment, animal carcasses and sealed sources of radioactivity which have been reduced to unuseable levels by the natural process of radioactive decay. These are hot wastes. They have been sealed in metal containers whose


life is estimated at only 10 years in sea water, and dumped in 250 feet of water off Boston.
I think we as Canadians have the right to ask probing questions about the safety of such an operation. What effect will this have upon our fisheries, and what plans has the atomic energy commission for other dumps? I have reason to believe that due to public pressure the atomic energy commission will not continue dumping near Boston, but have moved their operations to a site located 200 miles east of Cape Cod, while another site is proposed for an area 120 miles southeast of Sandy Hook, New Jersey. What effect will these hot waste dumps have upon our scallop industry, the largest and most vigorously expanding shell fishery in the maritime provinces?
Taking an example of the rate of growth of that industry, last year for the period from January to October the Canadian fleet alone landed 4 million pounds of scallops as compared with 2,900,000 pounds for the same period in 1958, an increase of approximately 40 per cent. These shell fish bring to our fishermen a landed price ranging between 35 cents and 40 cents a pound.
At the present time Canadian scientists are working with United States scientists to ascertain methods of improving the scallop fishing and reducing the number of small unmarketable scallops. These joint Canadian-United States studies are being carried out at the request of the international commission of the northwest Atlantic fisheries because the bulk of these scallops are caught on Georges bank, which is located in an area approximately 200 miles from Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, and 150 miles from Cape Cod, not very far from the atomic disposal dump.
As long as these atomic wastes remain sealed there can be no danger of contamination to our fisheries, but these containers will not withstand for an indefinite period the effects of salt water from without and hot wastes from within. In view of the value of our fisheries to present and future generations who must of necessity, as population increases, turn to the sea as a source of low cost protein food, I would suggest to our government that this matter of dumping hot atomic waste in the sea be taken up immediately with the atomic energy commission.
We should demand clear proof that dumping operations near the fishing banks used by United States and Canadian fishermen will be safe and will not generate future harmful effects for our resources or our people. If this proof is not available every effort should be made to stop this practice and have these atomic wastes buried in land that is nonproductive. In Canada atomic wastes from the

Chalk river development are sealed in containers similar to those used in the United States and dumped in the Ottawa river. The effects of this action should also be studied.
In my earlier remarks I mentioned that some of my constituents are engaged in forestry work. In addition to logging operations many supplement their income by cutting and selling pulpwood to the Bowater-Mersey Paper Company Limited at Liverpool. This company only recently came under the international Bowater's umbrella, and every effort is being made to increase production and sales.
When consideration is given to the value of the pulp and paper industry in Canada, it is very gratifying to me that the speech from the throne indicates that a new forestry department is to be established. This department is to be concerned with affairs relating to the forests of Canada and their most effective utilization and conservation, and is to assume responsibility for related resources. It is fitting that recognition be given to this industry. Pulp and paper create more wealth in Canada than any other single industry, representing some 35 per cent of the total value of our exports.
In my riding large areas of timber land are still individually owned. However, present tax laws do not encourage further timber development. For example, many lands are assessed by municipalities according to the value of the standing timber. The owner at the present time pays high taxes and is encouraged to cut his wood. After the valuable wood has been removed the land will be assessed for only a fraction of the value at which it was assessed when it contained a good stand of timber. The true value of the land, however, is its capacity to produce a continuing crop that can find a market, so it is to be hoped that taxation methods will be developed that will encourage owners to maintain and improve their woodlands.
Another important forest problem is silviculture or reforestation, which is a young science in Canada. The best methods of growing and managing forests have not yet been completely determined; nor has the question been answered, who should pay the costs for the silvicultural management of Canadian forests as a whole. At present there are two groups carrying out silvicultural activities in Canada. The first includes the federal and provincial governments. They are concerned mainly with the principles affecting tree growth, but the time, money and effort expended are small in relation to the need. The second group carrying out this work is the pulp and paper industry. This latter body is composed of experienced foresters, engineers and others interested in the
The Address-Mr. Crouse improvement of forest management and operations. However, their expenditures can only be made from profits, and their investment in new forest growth can only be made on the basis of the return received. You might also call their investment one in faith, for it is not possible to receive a return on the investment for at least 50 to 100 years, as it takes this much time to grow a completely new forest.
How can we assist in this work as a government? First, there should be closer liaison between the federal and provincial governments. Federal assistance in the field of reforestation and in nurseries should also be increased. Research should be undertaken and studies made for the development of wider markets for the by-products of the forest, including slash, bark and small sticks.
I believe our greatest contribution could be made by further participation in forest fire protection. We have made a start in this direction by encouraging forest access roads, and I believe this program should be expanded and accelerated when consideration is given to the benefits produced.
Those of us who represent maritime ridings will watch with interest the outcome of the second United Nations conference on the law of the sea. This conference is to be held in Geneva during March or April of this year. In view of the highly controversial actions taken by Iceland and other nations in extending their territorial and fishing limits unilaterally, without prior agreement with other nations concerned, I believe Canada's attempt to give leadership in this all-important matter is worthy of special mention. Under the capable direction of our Secretary of State for External Affairs a booklet has been prepared outlining the Canadian proposal, and I know it is the sincere hope of all Canadians that this will provide a basis for negotiation that will eventually result in agreement among all nations regarding the breadth of the territorial sea as well as fishing limits.
I do not believe the importance of this coming conference is realized by most Canadians. Without some agreement among the international community of nations the actions taken by Iceland will spread to other nations; and the existing situation, with British trawlers fishing under the protection of armed frigates, is anything but satisfactory. A recent visit to Canada by a three-man delegation from the British trawler federation to study the Canadian proposal prior to the conference would indicate the importance attached to this problem by the British.
I was privileged to meet with this delegation, and in their opinion the implementation of Canada's proposed 12-mile fishing limit
638	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Crouse would curtail their fish landings by an estimated 30 per cent, thereby throwing some 25,000 Britons out of work. The importance of the fishing industry to Britain is understandable when we realize that Britons eat some seven times as much fish per capita as Canadians, whose per capita consumption is only about 13 pounds per year. However, in my opinion, after talking with this delegation, the British are prepared to make some sacrifices provided a satisfactory solution to this problem can be found.
The implementation of this proposal as put forth by our Secretary of State for External Affairs is most important to the Atlantic provinces from a conservation point of view. At the present time we enforce the 12-mile limit on our own nationals while permitting all other nations to fish within three miles of our shores. Maritimers generally have not raised a serious objection to this law, as fishermen from the United Sitates are the most affected and the United States takes annually some 80 per cent of our fish exports. In keeping with the policy of our government, we in the Atlantic provinces wish to make our contribution toward maintaining friendly relations with our neighbours to the south. However, in the event that agreement is not reached at Geneva this year I would suggest to our government, in all fairness to Canadian fishermen, that the present regulations be amended and Canadian fishermen be given the right to fish within three miles of the Canadian coast, which is the privilege granted to fishermen of all other nations.
At the present time, Mr. Speaker, the most important problem facing our fishing industry in Canada is the cost of replacing fishing draggers, trawlers and equipment. The average age of maritime trawlers over 100 feet in length is approximately 10 years, and it is necessary for those engaged in the industry to adopt a replacement policy if we are to maintain our competitive position in foreign markets. Those replacements of necessity must be larger ships with increased power and larger deck winches, as it is necessary to travel greater distances and fish in deeper waters in order to catch fish on a year round basis.
At the present time we have the A. T. Cameron, a 177-foot trawler type research ship operated by the Department of Fisheries and used in Atlantic and Arctic waters. This ship is fitted with five laboratories, each fitted out with modern equipment and gear for various research procedures as well as oceanographic, hydrographic and survey work. I think the provision of this ship was a move in the right direction, as we 

know very little at present about the wealth of food that can be harvested from the sea.
However, the fishing industry generally will be unable to avail itself of the deeper water fishing areas discovered by the A. T. Cameron, for present ships are not equipped for long distance deep water trawling. In other words the knowledge gained from expensive and extensive research will not be fully utilized.
This situation of course cannot last indefinitely and some firms are already planning on expanding their fleets. At least one firm, Booth Fisheries Canadian Co. Limited, is planning on the addition of three new steel trawlers to their North Atlantic fishing fleet. These ships will be 133 feet in length and will have a carrying capacity of 400,000 pounds of fish. While this addition will increase the number of pounds of fish landed and provide further employment ashore and afloat, it is unfortunate that due to excessive costs these ships could not be built in Canada. I am informed that they will be built in the Netherlands, and other large Canadian fishing companies are planning similar action.
The reason for this is obvious when a comparison of costs is made. These ships will cost in the vicinity of $300,000 in the Netherlands while Canadian yards require about $600,000 for similar ships. From these facts it is evident that some thought must be given to assisting and stimulating the construction of commercial fishing vessels in Canadian shipbuilding yards. Our friends across the border are faced with a similar situation and congress has passed a subsidy bill under which the government will pay up to one third of the cost of building a new vessel. While details of the payments under this bill must be worked out between the house and senate committees, nevertheless it is indicative of the aid that is planned for the United States fishing and shipbuilding industries. This program will also increase their production and could provide a threat to our export markets.
To date the government has made an outstanding contribution to the housing industry, as was indicated by my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton South (Mr. McDonald) in his remarks this morning. I think they can make a similar contribution by assisting in the construction of ships in Canada. I believe that the first step is to make a close study of the problems besetting the shipbuilding and fishing industries. From discussions I have held with those who are familiar with the problems it would appear that the best incentive the government could give the Canadian fishing industry for the building up of a modern fishing fleet would be to institute investment allowances as is now being done

in the United Kingdom. These investment allowances would apply irrespective of the country in which the ship is built, with a higher allowance permitted on ships built in Canadian yards.
Increased depreciation should also be extended to existing fishing boats provided the allowance is used for the construction of new boats. This is necessary because a 100-foot wooden ship built in 1945 at a cost of $150,000 can only be depreciated for this amount while replacement costs in 1960 of a similar ship are $300,000. This type of program if implemented would be a great step forward for the Canadian Atlantic coast fishing industry. It would be the easiest and least costly for the government to administer and would revitalize the shipbuilding industry as well as assist in modernizing the fishing fleet.
When speaking in the house recently my colleague, the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates), mentioned the need to reestablish the ferry service between Kingsport and Parrsboro, Nova Scotia. In my opinion he presented the need for establishing this service in a very capable manner. The desire of all Nova Scotians to overcome some of our geographic handicaps is readily understood when an examination is made of the area and the distance from our east coast ports to our American and central Canadian markets. I should like to endorse his suggestion with respect to the implementation of this service as it would be of considerable assistance to fish exporters in my riding who are desirous of shortening the route to Amherst. For example, refrigerated trucks could leave Chester Basin and, travelling via New Ross, Kentville and the ferry, could cut off some 66 miles compared with the former route travelled. This would speed up delivery of our fish and produce by truck to other markets and I would urge the government to give every consideration to this proposal which will further strengthen the economy of our province.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. R. Granger (Grand Falls-While Bay-Labrador):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by congratulating the mover (Mr. Morissette) and seconder (Mrs. Casselman) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They maintained the traditions of the house in the quality of their speeches and acquitted themselves well.
I welcome this opportunity to place before the house some of the problems in my district. High in the priority of needs is improved communications on the Labrador coast. During the long winter and spring the coast of Labrador is almost completely isolated. Apart from the mail planes and the planes operated by the Newfoundland government for the
The Address-Mr. Granger International Grenfell Association, all transportation as such ceases when the C.N.R. coastal steamers make their last trips in the fall.
The only means of communication for most settlements is by small radiotelephone sets maintained mostly by the Department of Transport, and only some of the Labrador settlements have these. There are in fact fewer sets operating now on the Labrador coast than at the time of confederation of Newfoundland with Canada. I should like to impress upon the house the vital need for one of these sets in each community. At the present time, in the event of illness it is sometimes necessary to go by dog team eight or ten miles to the next village in order to get a message to a doctor or nurse. In some cases it is well nigh impossible.
The Department of Transport is doing excellent work at their large stations such as Cartwright but too few of the smaller settlements on the Labrador coast have any means of communication at all. May I express the hope that this year the Department of Transport will correct this deficiency.
I am well aware, and indeed in fairness I should point out that the Department of Transport is, and for many years has been, engaged in huge enterprises at the airports at Goose and Gander, both in my riding, and while these mighty contributions to international transport and national defence must be paramount considerations I would ask the minister not to overlook these smaller matters concerning the little people where the very lives of Canadian citizens are at stake and which could be remedied at very little cost indeed. I would invite his personal attention to this matter.
I would also request increased power for the C.B.C. radio station at Goose Bay so that settlements along the northern coastline can receive the station. A stronger station broadcasting educational programs to supplement the missionary work in education in these remote places would be of vast benefit.
There was a time when the Labrador cod fishery was carried on both from the shore and by floaters, the latter term being applied to schooners sailing from Newfoundland which fished in Labrador waters and carried their catch back to the island for processing and export. About nine or ten years ago, during a period when the type of fish produced by the floaters was not in demand, the Labrador floater fishery disappeared, and with the passing of the Labrador schooner there disappeared a way of life and an important part of Newfoundland's economy. Nowadays the shore fishery on the Labrador is still important but the ships of other nations are reaping the wealth of Newfoundland-Labrador waters.

The Address-Mr. Granger
The industrialization of the salt codfish business, resulting in keener competition and shortages of raw material for fish plants, must inevitably mean attention focusing once again on the prolific waters of the Labrador. I predict that in the future the salt codfish processing plants in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia will have to look increasingly to Labrador for supplies. I think Labrador fishery tailored to meet modern needs is a necessity. I would ask the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) to take a careful look at the possibilities of developing this abundant fishery for Canadian uses rather than leave it for our foreign competitors.
The community stage program is commendable, and I should like the Department of Fisheries to continue this program and include the Labrador coast in it. I should like to see a long range program of, say, ten community stages per year instituted.
A shortage of bait is a perennial handicap to the fishermen in my riding. I am glad to be able to say that a program of bait service has been instituted by the Department of Fisheries. I ask the Minister of Fisheries to continue to give this vital matter his sympathetic attention and to enlarge the program so that a complete bait service is available to Newfoundland and Labrador. Each year thousands of quintals of fish remain in the ocean because of a lack of bait. The national economy and the individual fishermen are both the poorer as a result.
Some day I hope to see a causeway across the strait of Belle Isle, providing a physical link between the mainland and the island of Newfoundland. This would really be the consummation of confederation. The possible effect of such a causeway from the standpoint of climate should be studied. There should be a determination made as to whether, in fact, such a causeway would divert the Arctic current away from the east coast of Newfoundland as well as blocking it from the gulf of St. Lawrence; whether the waters of the gulf would be warmer if Arctic ice were shut out; whether the ice that makes in the St. Lawrence river and gulf would continue to cool the climate in spring and whether there is a possibility that the climate of the whole maritime provinces might be improved by the deflection of the Arctic current. These are interesting speculations which might have far-reaching consequences. I would suggest that a working model be made and the possibilities of such a causeway explored now. This is an age of giant endeavour and the magnitude of the task should not discourage exploration. I suggest the minister of northern affairs give this matter serious consideration.


Of course, in time, I should like to see the trans-Canada highway built on the causeway, but I think the major concern at the moment is the possibility of improving the climate of the Atlantic provinces, with the possibility of added economic advantages. In my opinion it is a fascinating possibility, and I should like to see it given scientific study. Perhaps atomic power could be harnessed to throw up the huge barricade. If such an operation were attempted, it would be an atomic blast for peace.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention the desirability of rewriting the trans-Canada highway agreement with the provinces. In my opinion, in so far as the province of Newfoundland is concerned, the present 50-50 arrangement is not realistic. Total population, distances involved and capacity to pay should be taken into strict account. Newfoundland has a small population, and the distances involved are comparatively great. The province is not wealthy. I believe the per capita mile of the trans-Canada highway in Newfoundland is the greatest, or close to the greatest in Canada. The cost to the province is a grievous burden. I would make a plea that the government give urgent consideration to the possibility of modifying the trans-Canada highway agreement with the provinces so that the proportion of cost will be more equitably distributed. Perhaps no single project has greater potential for enriching and welding this nation together than the trans-Canada highway. I do hope that steps may be taken to hasten its completion, and the only way that will be possible for Newfoundland is by the government of Canada assuming a larger and more equitable share of the total cost.

Last year, as I recall it, he gained a good deal of notoriety for suggesting we were not paid well enough. This year he seems to be not so sure about that. He appears to have heard some expressions of doubt on that subject, and I was not quite sure where he finally left us. I was very interested to know, however, how he valued members of parliament. This seems to me to be a question which we might all really consider. If we are to have price tags, then it seems to me we should know how they are to be given. We should know whether, for example, a man gets so much for everyone who stays in to listen to him; whether he gets so much more for everyone who stays in and who does not read a newspaper; whether he gets so much for every question; whether he gets so much if a question is deemed, by a competent tribunal, to be a witty question.
The hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Houck) took a different line. He did not go in for the value of speeches, but he considered the cost. This is an interesting point, too. This raises another interesting question as to whether, if you were offered the $600 right away, on the nail, before you spoke, you might say, I do not believe my speech is worth that, so I will take the $600. I will take it in my stride. We will wait for these voices. As I say, if he liberates Canada in three years, I myself will put it down much more to Mr. King than I will to anybody else.
As I said, I am not going to go around the course again. I am not going to repeat things which have been said in criticism of the opposition because I want to turn to something different.
I was interested, of course, in those parts of the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) which were controversial and which dealt faithfully with the opposition. However, I was even more interested to note that they were not content just to say that everything in the garden was lovely, that we are having a properous year but that they went out of their way to warn us that there were very serious problems facing us and that we should be astute and watchful to meet them.
Some of these speeches were made in the House of Commons and some were not made in the house. For instance, the Prime Minister referred to Khrushchev's boast in which he said he was going to bury the west economically through production and trade. Again the Prime Minister referred to economic and trade forces "of hurricane proportions being launched against the free world." Those are words that I think we might all remember. He spoke again of the danger of the soviet world selling abroad at unreasonable terms dictated by political consideration and selling into our traditional markets.
I now want to come to the Minister of Finance. After urging that we pay attention to the danger to our foreign trade, he said this:
We are so dependent upon foreign trade, and so closely linked in many ways with the fortunes of the United States and our other trading partners

that we are bound to be affected, for good or ill, by the swings of economic activity originating outside our own borders.
My purpose this afternoon and the sole point of my speech, if there is one, is that we should not leave this entirely to the government alone. The great Lord Lothian once said in the United States that in a democracy responsibility comes clearly down on the shoulders of each and every one of us. That is something we should remember. Public opinion should always be alert and astute because, as we still know, public opinion can govern a nation. As I said, it should not be left to the government alone. Speaking to the Canadian Manufacturers Association the Prime Minister used these words which I should like to quote:
I would urge you to create whole new industries to produce things we have never seen before. The businessman as the great innovator can do more than just stabilize the economy-he can change its entire course. Canadian businessmen, as well as the nations political leaders need an Elizabethan sense of grand design-the vision and faith on which the future of nations and fruitful enterprise is built.
I want to quote a word here from a Canadian businessman Rhys Sale. Speaking the other day in Vancouver, Mr. Sale said things that interested me very much coming from a Canadian businessman, because often I feel there is a great tendency among Canadian businessmen to rely consciously or unconsciously on the maxim "Nothing is but thinking makes it so," and to say things which they like to hear. But Mr. Sale spoke out very clearly. He spoke about world trade and he spoke about a new dimension and- this is a thing we should all recognize-"a fantastic renaissance of European, Asiatic and African competition." I feel that if we do not take this seriously we are just not being realistic. He used other searching and eloquent words. He said that Canada faces a major challenge to its "growth and survival." No wonder the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) is calling for an Elizabethan sense of grand design. I commend those words of Mr. Sale. Incidentally, the same day, came an indication from British Columbia that the industrial commission was also urging people to step out of the country and carry on business abroad. Mr. Sale also had another point I should like to mention. He spoke of the serious maladjustment of economic revenues, and said:
The benefits of economic growth must be fairly distributed between those who buy the products of industry, those who make them and those who simply supply the risk capital.
What are we doing? We are making gifts under the Colombo plan and I was glad the press yesterday reported a further indication 79951-0-41J
The Address-Mr. Macdonnell of help resulting from a meeting in Washington a couple of weeks ago. This new help, I understand, is in the form of grants. I want to refer to a couple of distinguished United States witnesses; first, to Dean Acheson, who urges America to step up aid to underdeveloped countries. He gives some astounding figures. He is talking of investment, and he says that the United States, in order to make investments comparable having regard to its economy with the British investment abroad of 1913 would have to do 30 times as much as it is doing at present. He does not suggest that the United States could do anything like that amount, but he does suggest they should be doing more than their present hand to mouth action.
I want to refer also to Paul Hoffman, formerly successful administrator of the Marshall plan, later president of the Studebaker Corporation and now head of the special assistance department in the United Nations. He says the world is shrinking so rapidly that there must be global development, and goes on to give some astounding figures, figures which make one feel uncomfortable. The less developed countries, he said, had a per capita income in 1950 of $110. They hoped to have raised this by the end of the fifties by about $20 which, he says very truly, is not enough. The increase in per capita income in the western nations between 1950 and 1957 amounted to $300, and the increase in the United States to $530.
I am not going to dwell on these figures, but they do make one feel terribly uncomfortable. I want to stress, however, the fact that Hoffman does not put forward his argument on the ground of humanitarianism. He puts it forward on the ground of investment. He says that if we do not assist the underdeveloped countries, if we do not assist in the development of new markets, it is going to be the worse for ourselves.
I shall not worry the house by giving figures in any detail, but he gives figures of the amount he thinks is required in order to assist the underdeveloped countries, and according to him it is something which should be within our capacity. He thinks the amount of $20 billion over the next 10 years, shared among the wealthier nations and added to his reckoning of $180 billion which would be produced by the countries themselves, would make up the $200 billion which would be required. He points out that according to the present figures Canada and the United States are themselves planning to spend $500 billion in this 10-year period on the matter of defence.
I want to draw attention to these words from Hoffman and also words from B. K.
644	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Macdonnell Nehru, the brother of the prime minister, who is India's commissioner general for economic affairs.
I want especially to refer to India because it is of special significance to us, first of all because of its size and, next, because of its key position. What India thinks today, the rest of southeast Asia might very well do tomorrow. At any rate it would be an influence; it might even hold the balance for or against communism. Second, I should like to refer to India because India is a fellow member of the commonwealth and, third, because it is in an exceptional position to make use of loans. I want to explain that. One of the important things is that loans be given to countries which can make use of them by reason of their political stability, their economic organization, their possession of skilled engineers, and so on. The argument could be made that India, with all its weakness, is in a position to do this. After all, the British when ruling India, allowed Indians freely into the civil service so that when they left many Indians were skilled administrators. They have a democratic system of government. I was in the Indian assembly a couple of years ago and it was interesting to observe that they were even more closely based on London than we are.
I have here a speech by B. K. Nehru begging for assistance from Canada and the other advanced countries and saying that India should be able to provide itself 80 per cent of what is needed, but that they do require assistance. The remaining 20 per cent, he says, will have to come from outside, mainly in the form of loans and substantial amounts in the form of United States agricultural commodities and so on. Then he speaks very strongly. He says:
There are many factors which are required for economic growth and the chief among them are a stable government, an efficient and honest administration, managerial and organizational ability, technical competence and capital.
And again:
What is holding up India's development is, therefore, the shortage of capital and of nothing else.
He goes on to urge private investment, saying that the climate of India is favourable to it, and he stresses another point very strongly. As to profits, he says:
As to profits, those of you who have any experience of India would bear me out that the opportunity for profits for any reasonably well-managed concern is enormous. Demand is continuously and rapidly rising and the market is virtually completely protected for with our present shortage of foreign exchange, which will continue, we have perforce to limit our imports to those commodities which are essential and are not produced in India.


I had not thought of that before and it seems to me to be a very strong point addressed to the investor.
As I said to you, the annual report of the department of industrial development of British Columbia recommends to firms in British Columbia that they try to establish branch plants in Europe. That has reference to Europe, but there is no reason why it should not extend to other areas.
The great question is this. Here again let me remind you that according to Hoffman, it is self-interest and the building up of foreign trade of which we should be thinking. The great question is whether we are the kind of people who will do it. At this point I wish to read a short extract from an article written by that able woman, Barbara Ward, who was at one time an editor of The Economist. This is a paragraph which I think everyone should read, mark, learn and digest. I believe there is a great danger if we ignore these broad considerations and that if we do, we may years from now wake up and wonder if we were not like children playing in the sand. This is from an article which appeared in the New York Times a few weeks ago. Here is what she says:
As the world enters the nineteen sixties one fact seems sure. The pace of revolutionary change in every sphere of human affairs will gather momentum.
The breakthrough accomplished in the fifties in weapons, in space research, in every type of scientific advance: the political breakthrough of a score of new nations; the emotional breakthrough of a third of humanity hungering for economic growth-all these forces will expand explosively to make the sixties a period of challenge and change unequalled in human history.
What, in these circumstances, will be the response of the western powers? The answer depends not only upon the new political leadership available in the west. It depends profoundly upon the sort of people the free nations have become as they face the mounting crises of their age.
So we return to the question, what sort of people are we? I suppose it is fair to say that when we look at the underdeveloped countries we cannot possibly look at them purely as a business problem because, after all, we are humane people and the spectacle of hundreds of millions of people starving is appalling to us. I want to stress again that Hoffman whom I heard speaking in Toronto in October put it forward on the grounds of self-interest and the building up of foreign trade. I read to the house what Mr. Sale said about this stupendous competition which is arising not only in Europe but in Asia and Africa. The Prime Minister mentioned it too. Therefore, I ask whether people of intelligence can ignore these things?
I suggest that the government is entitled to the support of public opinion. I have already referred to the item in the press

today based on what was done in Washington recently whereby loans are going to be made. As far as I am concerned, I regard that with enthusiasm and I hope the public will regard it with enthusiasm. I hope the government will not be left to feel that it is away ahead of the procession and the response is only grudging. I hope that public opinion expressed through such agencies as the churches and educational and business institutions will make it clear that the people of Canada are back of the government in indicating that we cannot tolerate distressed, hungry and cold conditions among ourselves and that when it happens among other people it also leaves us moved.
I will conclude my remarks by saying this. We should base our thinking on what we know ourselves and on what was said by these distinguished United States writers I have quoted who have made a study of the question and base it also on the action of our own government which has some of the most able experts in the world to advise it. I hope that we as members and the people of Canada will look at this realistically and recognize this great danger described by a well known journalist who asked the question whether we are tough enough to face Russian competition in peace. He stresses the great danger for us in our present soft society where we have so much comfort and so much in the way of amusement that we may not be able to take things seriously.
All I can say is that I hope it is not so. We have been able to take things seriously up to the present time. No one is able to suggest that in war time we did not realistically face the serious issues that confronted us. No one can suggest that the Canadian people were not capable in those days of carrying burdens and making the sacrifices that were necessary.
If we do not look at the present situation in the cold light of its challenges, if we are not impressed by what the Prime Minister has said, if we are not influenced by the United States writers I have quoted, if the words of Barbara Ward I have cited fail to move us, then I earnestly suggest that the time may come when we may look back on this decade which we are assured is so tremendous in its possibilities and wonder if we were not like children playing in the sand. However, I did not intend to put those figures on the record because I am always reluctant to quote figures, especially when they tend to disprove opinions voiced by my hon. friends.
Even so, there was unemployment in this country in 1948. The proportion was 3.2 per cent, then it went up to 4 per cent in 1949 and to 6 per cent in 1950.
As the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) said in this house a few days ago, that is on Friday, January 29, the Korean war in 1950 helped to relieve the problem, one for which the government of the time was responsible to a certain extent.
The cycle again operated in 1951: the proportion was 3.3 per cent, then it increased to 4 per cent in 1952, decreased to 3.4 per cent in 1953, to increase again to 6.1 per cent in 1954, and to 7.4 per cent in 1955.

Yet at the time, that is in 1955, no solution was proposed; in fact, there were no complaints from members of the government in power. I might address myself in particular to the hon. member for Hull, who appears to be following my remarks with special interest -for which I thank him-and ask him this question: Why, since the fall of the former government, have attempts been made to display before the Canadian people a situation intentionally described as deplorable, while under the Liberal administration, before the Conservative government came into power, things were even worse, according to figures from the dominion bureau of statistics? I might say that the present government has made commendable efforts to improve the situation. It has tried, for instance, to suggest so-called winter works to every municipality in the country, without encroaching upon provincial jurisdiction.
This new venture has been criticized by the opposition, but the record is there to show that winter works have afforded relief to the people.
In addition to this step taken by the Conservative government, may I also mention that the Department of Labour is now very effectively persuading unemployed workers to take up special training courses. Those people may take those courses-there are 500 of them and even more-and continue to draw unemployment insurance benefits.
Well, Mr. Speaker, that is certainly a measure designed to improve the situation in the country, thanks to this government.
A moment ago I mentioned the winter works program. Last year that program made
40,000	additional jobs available to Canadians and to date this year more than 34,000 Canadians got employment that way.
I feel that the government deserves credit for its action and, since the hon. members opposite want figures showing at least the situation, I can say that the number of Canadians working this winter is 18,000 higher than last year.

The Address-Mr. Lafreniere
So, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to dwell any longer on this aspect of my remarks, but I simply want to stress the fact that those who are here, on parliament hill, should create among the public-which would indeed be in accordance with the facts-an atmosphere of optimism and confidence which, added to the work and effort of the government, would improve conditions.
May I, as we often hear critical comment on the subject, remind the house of the wise decision taken last year by the Conservative government to abandon production of the CF-105, which, to my mind, has not been sufficiently discussed in this house. May I, therefore, Mr. Speaker, recall an excerpt from an article by a journalist of the name of Lorenzo Pare, which was published on January 22, in the paper L'Action Catholique.
That article which I am quoting in part, says:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker took the risk. His decision provoked a storm, even among his most faithful followers. But the government persevered in its decision. The most recent developments- and more particularly the decision of Soviet Russia to abandon the traditional air force in favour of missiles-proved that Mr. Diefenbaker was right.
Canadians will not fail to note it. For the true measure of a government is in such acts of courage, accomplished in spite of great difficulties.
Mr. Speaker, I too want to congratulate the government for taking that decision.
I do not want to criticize the previous government too strongly for making decisions in 1945 which cost billions of dollars to the country for national defence purposes and which proved almost useless.
We should at times keep in mind certain basic principles, Mr. Speaker, and there is one which says that to govern is to foresee. At that time, the government had not foreseen, and we must be thankful that the present government, in spite of rumours heard last year concerning the decision it was about to make, had the courage to cancel the CF-105 in order to avoid unnecessary expenditures to the Canadian people.
It is with this remark, Mr. Speaker, that I want to bring this short speech to an end. I hope I shall have the opportunity when other items are under consideration to point out once more the lack of consistency and the lack of vision shown by those who are today in the opposition, regretting as they do their failure to adopt measures they insist we should be taking today. They express regrets

over the past and the present gives them little cause for comfort in the cold region of the opposition.

I know that last summer you represented our country in many other areas of the world, and those who accompanied you-at least, those I know-did not hesitate to say that you did so with great dignity, which did not surprise me at all.
I should also like to congratulate, even if it is a little late in the debate, the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn) on his appointment to the deputy speakership of the house. As did my colleagues, I too would like to welcome the two new members who have joined us lately, that is the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac (Mr. Webb) and the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Tardif).
And in closing my congratulations, Mr. Speaker, I should like to pay tribute to the two new ministers who are now part of the cabinet, and congratulate all parliamentary secretaries who have been nominated, during the parliamentary recess.
Mr. Speaker, yesterday evening, I listened very carefully to the stump speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), who told us at the beginning of his remarks that the speech of the Leader of the Opposition was meaningless. Yet, the Minister of Finance, Mr. Speaker, spent all his time refuting everything the Leader of the Opposition himself had told us, when he spoke during the debate on the address. The Minister of Finance, as usual, went in for sarcasm and irony. Now I know that sarcasm and irony are usually what people fall back on when they are

short of genuine arguments, and I know that it is the favourite argument of the Minister of Finance.
I know the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister, their cabinet colleagues and every Conservative member in this house hate to be reminded of their solemn pledges to the Canadian people in the 1957 and 1958 elections. We often hear this objection: "What did you do when you were in power?" However, that is beside the point, Mr. Speaker. When the hon. members opposite came to the people in 1957 and 1958, they told us of the problems which, in their view, were threatening Canada's economic life, and said to the Canadian people: "Put us in power, and we will put an end to those problems."
That is the reason why we are making a point to remind them of their promises, and to say: "Well, you committed yourselves to make this a better land to live in, so let's see you deliver the goods". That is what we are after. We were judged on our record, and we recognize it. But now, it is your turn to deliver to the Canadian people what you promised in the 1957 and 1958 elections.
When we picture Canada's present situation, we are accused of being prophets of doom. We are accused of speaking ill of Canada when we expose its true condition with respect to the economy, unemployment and other matters.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, when a child makes a mistake, I do not think it is running him down if you show him his mistake and tell him he should try to improve. You do not run down a child when you tell him his mistakes. And so, it is because we love Canada that we are drawing these things to the cabinet's attention and ask it to consider the problems and seek a way out. That is what we are aiming at.
We are not trying to run down the country. Oh, this is an expression I have often heard, "running down the province", but I repeat, when you want to help a child you are educating, I do not think it is running him down to show him his weaknesses and urge him to try to correct them.
That is what we are doing with this government.

Mr. Speaker, after analysing the promises that were made to the people of Canada in 1957 and 1958, I came to the conclusion that they were of two kinds. On the one hand there were promises that could increase our economic standard and, on the other hand there were other promises which appealed to the ideals, to the noble feelings of the Canadians.
May I first deal with those appealing to the noble feelings and to ideals, and then with those having to do with the economic life of our country.
This could be used as an appendix to a small book entitled "Two Years of Great Achievements". If we could publish those promises at the end of this small book, we would have the real picture of the situation in Canada, of the sincerity of our leaders and of the little care they show for the most solemn pledges they made to the people of Canada.
On April 25, 1957, according to a report in the Winnipeg Free Press of April 26, 1957, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker)., then leader of the opposition, had this to say:
(Text):
A Conservative government would abolish closure. (Translation):
On May 13, 1957, according to the same newspaper, dated May 14, 1957, the Prime Minister said this:
(Text):
A Progressive Conservative government would move to abolish the parliamentary rule of closure.
The Address-Mr. A. Brassard (Translation):
Here, Mr. Speaker, is one of the promises which, I believe, appealed to the noble feelings of the Canadians, to the desire and to this house. The Prime Minister, who had made this solemn pledge, has repeated it all across the country. However, we have not heard much about it since, except for a small resolution put on the order paper in 1958, as well as a reference made recently in the house, when he said: "Now that the Conservatives are in power, there is no longer a danger that this might be used". But why did he not tell the Canadians, in 1957: "If we come to power, we will never use closure", instead of giving them the solemn pledge of removing this rule from the statute books? I think that, perhaps unwittingly, the Prime Minister, misled the people of Canada when he made that solemn promise.
What did the Prime Minister have to say about the automobile tax during an election campaign? According to the Windsor Star of May 10, 1957, the present Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, said:
(Text):
Removing the excise tax would aid not only the automotive producers but also the feeder industry.
(Translation):
In Oshawa, home town of the Minister of Labour, the Prime Minister said on May 29, 1957, according to the Toronto Telegram of May 30, 1957:
(Text):
He told the automotive town audience his party would lift luxury taxes from cars because they are an essential part of public and private transportation. There is no more justification for a luxury tax on automobiles than there would have been for one on the horse and buggy 50 years ago.
(Translation):
That is what the Prime Minister said in Oshawa on May 29, 1957; and what did he do to fulfil his promise? He decreased it by 2\ per cent; but he had promised to lift it completely.
(Text):
Removing and lift.
(Translation):
In the words of my colleague from Shefford (Mr. Boivin):
When the Conservatives change places they also change faces.
And what did the then leader of the opposition say in Winnipeg, on May 14, 1957:
(Text):
The Conservatives, he said, would repair a serious omission in the federal health plan which does not include tubercular and mental institutions.
