Mr. Diefenbaker said the Conservative party still believes that hospital insurance should cover patients in mental and tubercular institutions.
(Translation):
What action has the Prime Minister taken to fulfil that solemn pledge, now that the Canadian people have given him their confidence, to an extent never seen before in Canada's political history? He has turned his back and has ignored his pledge to the Canadian people.
Here is what he said on tight money on February 19, 1957, in a speech to the Montreal chamber of commerce and I quote:
(Text):
Federal government expenditures constitute the biggest inflationary factor in our economy. Credit restrictions that have been introduced in our country apply only to individuals-They have forced provincial governments, municipal and school administrations to either discontinue necessary and vital improvements or pay excessive interest rates to finance them.
(Translation):
I also remember, Mr. Speaker, that when the Minister of Finance sat on this side of the house, he too used to speak with great feeling on the tight money situation. He cried over the plight of the small wage earner.
One might have expected, now that he is in charge of government finance, that there would be no more credit restrictions. However, restrictions were far less severe and far less serious under the former Liberal administration.
When the St. Laurent government handed over its powers to the present administration, I think it was on June 26, 1957 or rather on June 21, the rate on treasury bills was 3.81 per cent. Then it rose to 5.12 per cent and finally, on August 12, 1959 reached the alltime high of 6.16 per cent.
The Prime Minister keeps telling the Canadian people, either at public meetings or on television, that the Conservative government, his government, has no tight money policy.
When public bodies, corporations and small businesses started to react, he hastened to go on television and lay the blame on chartered banks, ignoring his own responsibility in this field as leader of the government and as Canada's first citizen.
Canadians, and even some Conservative party organizers, have realized the tight money situation. I need only refer, in this connection to an article which appeared last October 2 in the Toronto Globe and Mail reporting on a meeting of organizers and 

supporters of my good friend, the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee). The article had the following heading:
(Text):
Two Party Members Blast Fiscal Policy
A member of the Progressive Conservative party challenged Prime Minister Diefenbaker Wednesday night to disguise himself as a small businessman and try to get a bank loan.
The challenge came from Frank O'Byrne of the Agincourt Progressive Conservative association at an association meeting called to hear the member from York-Scarborough.
Mr. O'Byrne was commenting on a statement attributed to the Prime Minister recently when questioned about tight money. "Tight money? I don't know what it is,'' Mr. Diefenbaker is reported to have replied. "Mr. Diefenbaker," said Mr. O'Byrne, "should disguise himself as a small businessman and walk into any bank in this country and try to get a bank loan. He may be fooling himself about tight money but he is not fooling us," Mr. O'Byrne said.
(Translation):
I think that this evidence is much more conclusive and acceptable than mine is to my hon. friends opposite.
With regard to government policy on credit restrictions, I should like to read also a short article published in the September 7, 1959, issue of the Letter Review:
(Text):
Prime Minister Diefenbaker and Finance Minister Fleming have added nothing to the stature of the government or the enlightenment of the public by their recent utterances on the current tight money situation. This is unfortunate. It is unfortunate in the first place because both Mr. Diefenbaker and Mr. Fleming consciously, or otherwise, appear to be suggesting that the difficulties facing borrowers are mainly attributable to the policies of the chartered banks. This is both untrue and unfair.
(Translation):
Again on the matter of credit, Mr. Speaker, the Montreal Gazette, which is not necessarily friendly to the Liberal party, had this to say in an editorial dated October 5, 1959. Please note that this is an editorial and not a news report.
(Text):
The government cannot sit upon the fence and exhort or criticize others. Its own role in what has happened, and will happen, is very real.
For, as Royal Bank president James Muir pointed out recently, "it must be made clear to everybody that the Bank of Canada and not the chartered banks controls the volume of money and credit within our country-so long as the money supply is not allowed to increase with the demand for loans, the chartered banks must resort to the curtailment of loans through direct restriction (and rationing) of bank credit."
(Translation):
There is something else I want to say about the Bank of Canada. I very well remember statements made by the present Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister himself before June 1957. If my memory is correct, we had credit restrictions in 1955.

At that time, we really had a credit restriction policy, Mr. Speaker, because the Liberals who were then in power had the courage to make decisions and to make them known to the Canadian people.
The previous government, Mr. Speaker, was not in the habit of weighing each of its actions or each of its decisions according to the number of votes they might bring; its first objective was the welfare of the country and not that of the Liberal party.
About credit restrictions-indeed Mr. Speaker I am thinking again of the Bank of Canada-I repeat what I said on November 23, 1959 in a televised broadcast at home, that the Bank of Canada, if my memory is right, was set up by a Tory government, in fact, under the Bennett administration. If the government of today feels that the Bank of Canada is not discharging its functions properly, why then do the Minister of Finance and his cabinet colleagues not introduce amendments in this house-and it would be their responsibility to do so-why don't they introduce amendments to bring the Bank of Canada to play the part it should play in our economy?
Not very long ago, the city of Montreal borrowed $13 million at a 7.58 per cent interest rate. The city of Chicoutimi paid 6.49 per cent interest to float a $235,000 issue on November 10, 1959. On October 27, the municipality of McMasterville floated $443,000 at a net cost of 7.07 per cent. When this municipality borrowed money in 1955 it had paid only 4.01 per cent.
Interest rates are high, Mr. Speaker. In my humble opinion, those rates do not particularly affect the big companies since such interest is for the most part deductible for income tax purposes, the remainder I think being paid by the consumers at least on goods, on labour costs, through an increase paid by the consumers. It is not the same thing for small enterprises having but little capital. Nor is it the same thing for lower-bracket salary workers, because they have to pay for higher priced commodities or labour, as a result of increased interest rates.
Government representatives have always given us the impression that they were looking after lower bracket salary workers. And they like to repeat that in their speeches. But what are they doing today? What are they doing to correct a situation which is detrimental to lower salaried people, to small industries? If my memory serves me right, the Prime Minister of Canada, who was then leader of the opposition, said in Brockville, on May 8, 1957, in reference to small industries, as recorded in the Ottawa Journal of May 8 of the same year, the following:
The Address-Mr. A. Brassard (Text):
Canada, Mr. Diefenbaker said, might well follow the United States in encouraging small business. It could do so by offering technical assistance, granting loans and making defence contracts available to the little fellow.
(Translation):
In fairness to the Prime Minister, I must say that the government has set up a committee to consider the possibility of assisting small industry. But last year-I still remember-somebody asked the Prime Minister in the house if this committee would lend money to small business concerns. The Prime Minister then replied, I also remember, that at the time it was out of the question. His answer gave us the impression that possibly the committee might, in the future, lend money to small businesses. But this promise was made in 1957. When it was made, it was meant to influence the vote. People throught that if the leader of the opposition became prime minister and set up a committee to assist small businesses across the country, it would provide a new stimulus to the whole Canadian economy.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock? (Text):

Mr. Speaker,
shortly after the six o'clock adjournment, one of my friends, the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Brassard) told me that I had used yearly statistics, while I should have used monthly statistics.
Having read over the speech made by the Minister of Labour, I should like to quote a sentence which clearly shows that the statistics given by the Minister of Labour were for years and not months. It is to be found in the record of January 29, 1960, page 491, and I quote:
(Text):
I would ask the house to examine with me the unemployment figures during the years when the present opposition was in office when this cycle was developing.
(Translation):
I am very glad that the hon. member for Chicoutimi should have made this remark, because I am now able to complete what I had to say about unemployment.
In the eleven years during which the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) has been a member of the cabinet, the percentage of jobless people has been less than 3 per cent for seven years; as regards the other four years, it was about 3 per cent, for two years, and about 4 per cent for the other two years. It is therefore fair to say that the hon. mernoer for Essex East has no lesson to learn from the Minister of Labour.
And that also explains why it is so difficult for us to obtain from the Minister of Labour accurate statistics on unemployment, when we know that his own staff is unable to estimate the accurate percentage of jobless people who are seeking work in Canada.
While I am on this matter, Mr. Speaker,
I should like to point out to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) a situation which I have at heart, and which concerns my own constituency. It appears that the Canadian National Railways intend to have their cars repaired at Garneau station in future, while they are now being repaired at Chauvigny. Should that decision be implemented, Mr. Speaker, 50 heads of families in my constituency would be deprived of a job. I would therefore urge the Minister of Transport to reconsider the situation and see to it that unemployment does not increase in my constituency, where there are so many jobless people, both heads of families and young people who, through lack of work, are unable to earn their living.


I should like to say a few words to the hon. member for Dorchester with regard to Canada's external affairs. I would have liked to deal with other matters he discussed, but I shall refrain for lack of time. May I just read to him this statement from the Manchester Guardian for January 3, 1958, and I quote:

When the Liberals were defeated in June, the most common reaction outside Canada was regret that this meant the withdrawal from office of Mr. Pearson at a time when he had greatly enhanced his moral reputation and influence. All sorts of countries had learned to respect Canada as a nation which threatened no one but which had a mind of her own; which had pulled herself up by her own boots, but had no axe to grind.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to make my contribution to this debate. I want to offer my warmest congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address; the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Morissette) and the hon. lady, the member for Grenville-Dundas (Mrs. Casselman).
As I listened to the hon. member for Rimouski, my seat mate, I realized that here was a young Canadian already wearing the mantle of potential greatness. His potentialities were evident and much more will be heard from him in the future. Of the lovely lady from Grenville-Dundas, I would just say that she acquitted herself admirably and set a standard which will challenge the best of those who will take her place in the future. Her father and her constituents may well be proud.
Since I came to the house I think I have attended diligently. I have observed the members' conduct here and heard them in action. I think that perhaps my observations may be interesting to the house and I should like to say before I give them that, of course, they are made without prejudice. It is quite obvious that the giants of the opposition of yesteryear fitted into the seats of the ministry with much more ease and in a much abler fashion than those sad, sorry, forlorn, and frustrated souls who occupy the front benches of the opposition down here to my right. They have not yet realized that the Canadian public gave a verdict in 1957 and 1958. It just was not supposed to happen, and they have not yet got into the habit of being in opposition and doing the job they are supposed to do.
Some hon. members coming to this house in support of the government who have been put over here on the rump side and who rub shoulders with the deflated characters who sit over here may not be very happy to find themselves to your left, Mr. Speaker. But as a new member I have appreciated sitting on this side of the house because it has
The Address-Mr. More given me an opportunity to observe at first hand the great parliamentarians of the government benches in action.
I come from the wonderful province of Saskatchewan and I live in the capital city of Regina-the jewel of the prairie-an evergrowing jewel becoming greater and more sparkling every day and every year. I love my province, and I think my city is the finest place in the world in which to live and raise a family. It has been good to me for many years. I have spent all my life in my province; I have spent over 30 years in my constituency. I appreciate the confidence that they placed in me in sending me here in the election of 1958. I hope I will interpret their wishes in the manner in which they want them interpreted and I pledge myself to serve them in the most competent manner of which I am capable.
Sometimes when I listen to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) I wonder where in the world I have been living for 52 years.

speechtext: But the hon. member should not be one of them. The picture which the hon. member for Assiniboia paints of my native province is not the picture I have in my mind at all. It is completely incompatible with my experience and with the facts as I know them.

Pipe down, my friend; I have never interrupted you. I say that we have a great province and the finest people in the world. They are not whiners. They are not sorry for their plight. They are independent and resourceful and have contributed much to the development of Canada. I know they will carry their full share in the future development of Canada.
When they come to Ottawa to present their views I believe they have a perfect right to do so. We have had great areas of Canada grow under the benevolent protection of tariffs and the people of our province merely want to be given the same consideration.
From time to time I am informed that my friend the hon. member for Assiniboia goes back to my province and makes speeches and appears on television. He draws some fair audiences, too. It is interesting to hear the results of these and see how they are tabulated in certain quarters. According to the hon. gentleman we should not even be here, but I will leave it to hon. members of this house to determine whether or not the hon. member for Assiniboia is really the true voice

The Address-Mr. More of the prairies. We have 17 federal constituencies in that province. You can take a look at the membership representing the other 16 and decide for yourselves.
I have heard suggestions in this chamber, in the corridors and elsewhere to the effect that the throne speech debate is a great waste of time, that it is too long and does not contribute much of value, that it should be curtailed if not almost dispensed with. I am not one who agrees with those suggestions. A backbencher in this house does not get too much opportunity to participate in debates. The debate on the throne speech is one of the opportunities given to him to voice his views and to go freewheeling around his constituency or around the globe, if he likes. I think it is well worthwhile and that the backbencher is entitled to make his observations in this debate. Perhaps the 40-minute time limit is too long and could be reduced but certainly I feel that the throne speech debate should be continued for the length of time it now runs. If there is a move to cut 10 minutes from the speaking time of participants that could well be adopted and would serve the purpose of reducing speaking time and meet the criticism about waste of time.
Much has been said in this debate by the hon. members of the opposition about the omissions from the speech from the throne. They have been extremely critical, have spoken at length about it and treated us to many lectures on the subject. But I do not think they are making much headway because it is a weak attack. What does and will count with the people when they judge this session of parliament will be the accomplishments of the session. After all, there have been many throne speeches during the time this parliament has been in existence, many of them under a Liberal government, and in spite of the promises that were made in election after election by the Liberals we never heard in those throne speeches any mention of a national hospital insurance scheme or the South Saskatchewan river dam project. Here we are now after slightly over two years of Conservative administration and both these projects are in effect.
The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) is being very kind to me. I thought when I mentioned national hospital insurance and claimed that it was brought into effect by the Conservative government the hon. member would rise in his overexuberant, voluble fashion and defend himself by saying that the Liberals passed legislation for a national hospital insurance scheme.

speechtext: I did not want to interrupt your first speech.

I would have welcomed the hon. member's interruption because I wanted to remind the hon. gentleman that after the 1957 election when there were rumours that I might be successful on my second try at winning the election campaign the Liberals marched my hon. friend into Regina to bolster Liberal morale there. Of course, we were delighted and honoured to have him. He stepped off the plane in Regina and was very dignified, perhaps too dignified. A television fellow came up to him and welcomed him saying, "Mr. Martin, have you any comments to make?"
I am speaking from memory and I may paraphrase incorrectly but the hon. gentleman can correct me if what I attribute to him is wrong. The hon. member replied, "Why, my greatest concern at this time is that the Conservative party has no interest in hospital insurance. They have delayed and are making no progress. We passed the legislation and they have reached agreement with only one province. The Conservatives have no intention of following through because they do not want it."
The hon. member knows very well that we brought in agreements and the scheme became effective. We are all for it and are glad we have it.
Under this government much has been accomplished. In 1958 we went to the people and told them we had done the immediate things we thought were necessary to alter conditions in the country as they had been left us by our Liberal friends, those peerless hon. gentlemen who sat on the other side of the house for 22 years. They never got out of a scrape in all their years in office unless there was a total war or an event like the outbreak of hostilities in Korea that shook them out of their lethargy and got them off the hook. They never got out of any situation on their own.
I am not going to be like the columnist who on the front page of the newspaper under a byline said that the throne speech was meaty and full and it would be a long session, and in his daily column on the inside of the page said it was dull, empty and surely would not keep parliament very long. His ghost writers somehow just did not get together.
This has not been very dull for me up to date. There has been a lot of interest in this debate for me. One of the things that has been of real interest to me has been the final admission and publication of the fact that the great Liberal party is dead. Its demise has been acknowledged and admitted in the house by no less august a personage than the hon. member for Essex East, not once but twice. It has happened rather quickly. It is just

The Address-Mr. More
two months short of two years since we have been in office. It happened, as I say, extremely quickly. It is less than two years since they came from that great position of power which they felt was eternally theirs, given them almost by divine right and guaranteed for life. They then moved over to this side of the chamber to sit next to the small group of C.C.F'ers. We did a pretty good job of eliminating the splinter parties as they used to be called and only one remains. We have one member from Saskatchewan. We might have got rid of him, but perhaps next time. There are a few others from British Columbia and Ontario but all told there are only eight. However, in two months less than two years this small group seduced the formerly powerful Liberal party and the Liberal party succumbed to them.
For years the greats of the opposition of yesteryear sat on this side of the chamber before they assumed office. Hon. members of the Conservative opposition in previous years had 25 or 28 of these C.C.F. self-styled socialists sitting beside them on this side of the chamber. They had to rub shoulders with them and sit next to them, but they were not seduced and they did not succumb because they believed in their policies and their ideals. Finally, they reached the position to which they were entitled and they will stay there for a long time.
Instead of having a party in opposition now, Mr. Speaker, we have just two groups. I shall leave it to those in the public galleries and the people of Canada to make up their minds as to which is the most effective of the two groups. The C.C.F. know what the job of an opposition is, but the Liberals sitting here have not yet admitted that they are not the ministry. They have not learned and all they give us is a bunch of lectures. I have had the honour of their visits to my constituency many times. All these greats and former greats who are now in opposition have come into my constituency. The hon. member for Essex East has been there and he is a good friend of mine. He even got a fellow to drive him a few miles out in the country where I live to see me, but I was not at home. I was not at the $5 a plate dinner either which he attended to put a floor under Thatcher and to help the Saskatchewan Liberal party get going. I heard they got $2,100 out of it, but they did not get it at $5 a plate. I do not know how much my hon. friend from Essex East put into the kitty but the fact is we have not heard a word about Thatcher since.
This debate has not been uninteresting to me at all. There have been some very good contributions to it, and one of those contributions that I found interesting was that
made by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). I had the opportunity to visit Japan last May. I spent a couple of weeks there. I saw in the resurgence of that country much to admire. They are under great pressure from the communist bloc, but they are resisting it with the strength that only free men in a free enterprise and capitalistic system can show. I found that they are great friends of Canada, and as their economy grows and as they develop it will present us with a great opportunity. With understanding and co-operation between our two governments I look with confidence to expanding trade on a mutually beneficial basis.
What about the communist world? In his speech the hon. member expressed the same old socialist nonsense. Every time you want something and the state does not look after you, then you are overwhelmed with anxiety and fear. I do not subscribe to that sort of nonsense at all. His only panacea is more statism. I am not a socialist. Surely, that is evident by now. I am not an apologist for our present capitalistic and free enterprise system because in this world as we know it there is no place on earth where the people have benefited more than those who live in the country of our neighbour to the south and those who live here in Canada. We have the second highest living standard in the world. That has been brought about under this free enterprise and capitalistic system that my friends always get up and apologize for.
They always say that it will not work. It is true it has its faults, but I ask the hon. member to tell me of one system in the world that has been more flexible and more able to correct its faults and go on to serve its people and do a better job than free enterprise. I say to the hon. member for Vancouver East that I am a firm believer in our free enterprise system and in the resourcefulness that it gives to the people who live under it and that with courage and working together as free men we have the ability and the will to meet any challenge, economic or otherwise, no matter where it comes from in this world as we know it today.
The hon. member went on quite a bit further. I was interested in what he had to say. I see where he gained some notoriety or notice in the paper. He said, "This is indeed a year for truth". I agree it could well be a year for truth. I do not know to whom he is implying dishonesty in past years, but I have a few questions I should like to ask my hon. friend. I think the people in Canada, and certainly the people in my province where there will be an election, probably in June, are very interested.

The Address*-Mr. More
I would like to ask him, what are the real objects and aims of this new party that is going to be put on the people as my hon. friend said in his remarks, from the top rather than from the bottom? What really are its aims and objects? He is giving his all to its formation, and giving it willingly. Is it to keep the cold class war going we have that pretty well taken care of in Canada. For years and years my socialist friends picked on the mortgage companies. Then it was the banks. Later it was private business. Now they stand up and say they are all for the little businessman.
I was a member of the retail merchants association in the early days of the C.C.F. They did not distinguish between them in those days. Any guy who was fortunate enough to make a little money and invest it and make a little profit in making his living, they were against him; they were out to get him. They have not changed so far as I am concerned. Then with the formation of this great new party-I see my hon. friend rising; I do not know, but maybe it is the voice of Stanley Knowles that is speaking-with respect to the formation of this great party, is it solely for the purpose of providing an exchequer for the next election which my hon. friends will have to face? Are they taking it out of the pockets of the labouring men to put it in the pockets of the hierarchy, so that they can put it in their coffers?
They talk about our publicity and our public relations. I leave it to the house to decide what would happen. They will have them screaming all over the country. Yes, Mr. Speaker, it is a year for truth. I am proud to belong to a party that does not believe in a nation whose people are divided because of race, colour, class or creed but believes in one people and one nation, free and courageous and capable of meeting the challenge of this decade and building to greater heights than ever before.
I believe, regardless of what the hon. member who just resumed his seat said, that our stature in international affairs is continuing to grow under the wise guidance of our beloved and capable Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green). I want to be brief and at this time I only want to put on the record a quotation from the speech he made in Vancouver on January 4, 1960, to the advertising and sales bureau of Vancouver. I think he summed up the position very well when he said:
Now I come back to my text, that no nation faces a greater challenge in world affairs than Canada and that no nation has greater opportunity for leadership. Perhaps Canada could play a decisive role in bringing world peace. In any event, let us go into this new decade with the optimism and the courage and the strength of


character of our forefathers. If we do, I believe that Canada will end the decade as one of the leading nations of the world.
There it is again, Mr. Speaker. Not the fear and anxiety of socialists. More statism is their only panacea. I repeat, not the fear and anxiety of socialists but the opportunity, the challenge and the courage of free men in a free society.
I now want to turn briefly to a subject in which I am greatly interested and which is of great interest to the people of the prairie provinces, particularly of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. I am speaking now of a farm problem among other things. I am not a farmer. In our group we have many practical farmers who will say their piece. I want to speak on a subject that will bring benefits to the farmers of the prairies and that is the development of the port of Churchill. There are three doors open from Canada, as I understand it, to overseas trade and commerce. We have the door on the east coast and the St. Lawrence seaway; we have the door on the west coast with the harbours there; and we have a door which is the greatest door through which potential benefits of overseas trade could flow to the prairies, namely the door of the port of Churchill. I do not expect to get too much sympathy for my argument.
I do not expect too much sympathy for my argument from members of the Liberal party because in general they support their leader completely. Churchill is a little bit to the north and probably their view of it will be "from igloo to igloo". Any time they get away from the warmer regions of Canada to consider the north they look at it as nothing but igloos and igloos. The attitude used to be from tent to tent or from tepee to tepee when we were expanding from east to west but now it is from igloo to igloo as we go north. Such vision, such imagination, will never put them back where they think they have a divine right to be.
Churchill is past the stage of being an igloo town and it is going to go places. I have no criticism of the great developments that have taken place for the doors to markets in the east and in the west. But I do say in all seriousness that much of the problem we have in the prairie provinces could be removed if at this time the real potentialities of Churchill were considered and projects undertaken to develop them. I do not think this should be left to the government alone. I think private enterprise, business and corporations should give this matter their attention.
Churchill today is a thriving town of 1,500 people. It has schools, stores, hotels and an active chamber of commerce. It is the location of Canadian and United States military

bases and a rocket base and it has a five million bushel grain terminal. It has daily railway passenger service and daily air schedules from an excellent airport.
The open season for the port runs from July 25 to October 15 at the present time which is complementary to our harvesting and delivery season. With modern techniques and facilities such as radar, radio, ice patrols, helicopters and other marine aids, there is no reason why this season cannot be greatly extended. There is no longer to my mind any reason for maintaining the discriminatory differentials in freight rates and marine rates or for confining the area which can make use of this port to the present small area of the prairie provinces. I understand that the shipment of wheat through Churchill means an 11cent greater return to the farmer and 7 cents less charge to the consumer because the port is 1,100 miles nearer to Europe and our markets than shipping through the St. Lawrence seaway. That is a total saving of 17 cents per bushel.
I do not want to take too long, Mr. Speaker, because other members want to speak but I should like to refer to an article in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of September 24 where it is pointed out that ocean transport, provided the bottoms carry a full load, is the cheapest in the world. It is also pointed out that at that date 15,980,000 bushels of wheat had been shipped through Churchill in 42 vessels, or an average load of 380,475 bushels each and that direct shipments to Europe in ocean bottoms through Fort William had amounted to 13,500,000 bushels in 70 ships or an average of only 192,860 bushels in each ship.
I think the farmers of western Canada have a right to have their wheat delivered to market in a way that will bring the greatest return to them. I do not think that development at Churchill from now on will in any way affect the St. Lawrence seaway picture. I think its future is assured. The shipping that is going to come in and go out over that route will develop it. But in the meantime I do not think we should have to wait for development at Churchill.
I want to put on the record certain recommendations that have been made by the Hudson bay route association, a voluntary organization representing individuals, business, towns, villages, boards of trade, chambers of commerce, rural and urban municipalities and the provinces concerned. There is need at Churchill to make the most of these potentialities and the association points out that the first need is for additional grain storage space. Second, there is need for the extension of ship berthing and docking space.
The Address-Mr. Roberge Third, there is need for the shipment of grain from C.P.R. points to Churchill. The C.P.R. lines cross other lines where shipments of grain could be diverted over the Churchill route, and I see no reason why that cannot be arranged. Fourth, there is need for the establishment of competitive freight rates with respect to incoming freight on the Hudson bay line. Fifth, there is need for the extension of the marine insurance season at competitive rates. Sixth, there is need for an investigation into the possibility of establishing a port of transshipment in Newfoundland with storage facilities which would be open all year. Much more grain could then go through Churchill and could be placed in a position where it would be available for onward shipment throughout the year and not just for five or six months as is the case now in shipping through Churchill.
Finally, sir, I want to say a few words of appreciation to our Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the members of his cabinet. They are capable, earnest men with the vision and wisdom that the nation needs at this time. I have confidence in them and trust them. I feel sure from what I know, and I travel throughout my constituency and province a lot, that the people of Canada have that same trust in them. I pledge to them my loyalty and full support.

The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn) deserves congratulations on his appointment as Deputy Speaker of the house and your assistant, Mr. Speaker, as well as chairman of the committee of the whole house. I had the privilege of knowing the member for Quebec South when we were reading law together at Laval University, and my experience is that he will fulfil his new task with much dignity, wisdom and savoir-faire.
May I also, Mr. Speaker, congratulate the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Morissette) who very ably discharged the thankless task he had been called upon to do.
(Text):
I should also like to pay my compliments to the charming lady from Grenville-Dundas who made a very good contribution to this debate.
(Translation):
My hon. friend from Longueuil (Mr. Sevigny) should also be congratulated on his

The Address-Mr. Roberge appointment to the office of Associate Minister of National Defence. We wish him a great deal of courage and success.
(Text):
I should also like to congratulate the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Walker) on his appointment to the ministry in the capacity of Minister of Public Works.
(Translation):
One of the first problems, Mr. Speaker, with which I would like to deal tonight, concerns a situation now facing independent telephone companies. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has probably received, during the year, hundreds of letters from small independent telephone companies. You, yourself, Mr. Speaker, have probably received some from companies located in the vicinity of Quebec city.
The Independent Telephone Companies Association of Canada represents 650 telephone companies in Quebec and Ontario. Those companies serve more than 280,000 patrons, which is evidence of their importance in the economy of those two provinces. It also means that the government should help them out in some way or another.
At the time of the Liberal administrations of Mr. Mackenzie King and Mr. St. Laurent, independent telephone companies benefited from grants paid to them by the Department of Transport, when they proceeded with projects to improve their services or with some major repair work. The government came to their assistance through special grants as soon as the projects had been approved.
But since the Conservative party has been in power, the subsidies have been discontinued and the smaller independent telephone companies have to face very real financial problems.
I suggest that the government consider the possibility of restoring those grants to small telephone companies. If, on the other hand the government feels that this help is not justified, I suggest, as did those who wrote to the Minister of Finance, that the relevant provisions with regard to the Industrial Development Bank of Canada Act should apply to small independent telephone companies.
There is another problem upon which I want to draw the government's attention, Mr. Speaker, which more particularly affects the constituency of Megantic and deserves to be dwelt upon a few moments, and I now more particularly direct my remarks to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker). The town of Black Lake in my riding has two post offices, one being classified as rural and the other as semi-staff.
For this fiscal year 1957-58, the revenue of those two post offices amounted to $12,000.

Some people in the city of Black Lake feel that a public building should be erected to house the post office. If the government finds that such a building is necessary, I must warn public works officials to be careful in choosing an appropriate location for the proposed post office.
Mr. Speaker, in 1959 Robertsonville post office became a semi-staff office and, following the resignation of the ex-postmaster it was necessary to move the post office into a private home. Thus a public building is required also in Robertsonville and I urge the Minister of Public Works to note my recommendation.
Mr. Speaker, the most important problem facing the people of Megantic constituency, and more particularly the people of Thetford Mines, is that concerning asbestos.
The problem is of particular concern to me because it involves a large number of people in my constituency. I should like to deal with it from two angles: the production of asbestos, and Canada's external trade.
In view of the fact that this is probably the first time the problem has been discussed in this house. I think I might briefly go over the background of the situation.
Asbestos is not a new mineral. Its history goes back as far as Herodotus, the father of history. There was even mention of it at the times of Plutarch and of Marco Polo. It was identified in those days by its special properties rather than by its present name.
Asbestos was first discovered in Canada, around 1870, by a farmer named Jos. Fecteau, from the township of Ireland in Megantic county. In fact, a monument has been erected in his honour in the city hall square of Thetford Mines.
It was only around 1874, however, that serious efforts were made to extract this mineral from mines located in my area. Asbestos mining was quite different in those days from what it is today, and perhaps it might be interesting, in this connection, to quote from a publication entitled: "Asbestos, the strangest of minerals," published by the Quebec asbestos industry information service, in co-operation with the main asbestos mining companies:
In the very first days of asbestos mining in Quebec, the mineral was delivered to the market on horseback.
After being separated from the rock by means of tools, the fibres were put into small bags. From time to time, the miners, who doubled as farmers, took their horses out of the pasture and, having loaded the bags on their back, drove them through woods and swamps to the closest railway stop. In winter, transportation was easier; they used to put the bags on sleds drawn by oxen.

This transportation system lasted from 1875 to 1878, until a railway line was brought into the asbestos country. Since then, asbestos shipments have been an important and stable source of revenue for the Canadian railways.
The Quebec Central Railway has also benefited by it.
At present, asbestos deposits are mined by many companies, the largest being the Canadian Johns Manville, with head office in the town of Asbestos, in the constituency of my hon. friend the member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Dubois). In the district I have the honour to represent here, many companies share this natural wealth and co-operate with a view to efficient extraction. Evidently, this will extend the life of those mines and will give employment for many more years to increasing numbers of workers. For instance, during the last decade, the Asbestos Corporation Limited, the Bell Asbestos Mines Limited and the Johnson's Company Limited have joined forces to move part of the city of Thetford Mines in order to develop mineral deposits which before could not be mined because of the presence of the railway, the national highway and many houses.
The Quebec Central Railway line has been rebuilt a short distance from the asbestos deposits, for a length of about nine miles. Fart of the national highway which crossed the city of Thetford Mines has also been closed to the public. A new section of this highway has been built almost exclusively at the expense of those companies. As to the merchants or others who occupy mining sites, their commercial establishments or residences were transferred to another part of the town and hundreds of houses have now been moved in this way.
The whole move was almost entirely done at the expense of those mining companies who have spent at least $5 million on the relocation project. During the same decade, new plants have been set up, more particularly by the Asbestos Corporation Limited and by the Johnson's Company. This short list does not of course, take into account the new companies which have settled in the district, and more particularly the Flint-kote Company of Canada Limited, established about 1945, nor the Lake Asbestos of Quebec Limited, the National Asbestos Limited and Philip Carry Company in the riding of Beauce.
When the Prime Minister toured the province during the summer of 1959, he was able to see for himself at Black Lake, a town in the neighbourhood of Thetford Mines, the
The Address-Mr. Roberge tremendous work that had been carried out by the Lake Asbestos Company Limited, at the cost of $35 to $40 million, prior to going into operation. They had to dry up a lake there and remove large quantities of soil and sand, in order to uncover the asbestos fibre. It is said that they removed more soil and sand from that place than in the Canadian section of the St. Lawrence seaway.
This brief outline of ancient and recent history will show, therefore, the capital importance of the asbestos industry in that area of Quebec and Canada.
That fact,, however, was surely not unknown to the government and especially to the Department of Trade and Commerce, nor to the Department of Labour.
If I have chosen to deal with this problem today, it is that at least 800 asbestos miners are now jobless, and will remain so for a few months, and that, of course, raises a
problem of capital importance.
All these considerable outlays were made, as I have said before, in order to better our productive capacity and thus create jobs for more Canadians over a longer period. Unfortunately, conditions on the external market have not followed production trends.
If we read the reports of the commission an Canada's economic prospects and more particularly the volume entitled "Mining and Mineral Processing in Canada" by John Davis, we shall understand all the significance of that industry with regard to our export trade.
May I be allowed to quote some excerpts from this work. I quote the following from page 212:
Asbestos continues to lead by a considerable margin all other industrial minerals produced in Canada. Its value of production is currently in^the order of $100 million: that of gypsum, the next non-metal in line, is $7 million. All of ^Canadian produced industrial minerals together were valued at $145 million in 1955. These statistics, together with the fact that 95% of the nations asbestos output is exported (and is therefore an important earner of foreign exchange) underline the important part played by this industry in the

Over the years it has varied. Usually, it s ranged between 60 per cent and 70 per cent, eluding the U.S.S.R., it has historically run ound 75 per cent, though since 1945 it has shown
And he adds the following:
Increased competition is expected from countries *ehind the iron curtain. Already Russian asbestos 5 often offered at prices lower than Canadian and

The Address-Mr. Roberge Is sold for payment in local currencies under conditions of barter or within trade agreements negotiated between the governments concerned. At the expense of markets for Canadian long fibre, it has been freely exported to West Germany, France, Holland and Belgium. Although, traditionally, asbestos from this source has lacked care in treatment, present-day Russian fibre is well prepared for the market, of excellent quality and uniform in grade.
As indicated by the figures already quoted, Canada, properly speaking, has no asbestos products industry. We extract the mineral itself. And I quote here from page 221 of the same report:
Since the 1930's a modest asbestos products manufacturing industry has grown up in this country. Absorbing about 4 per cent of total Canadian mine output, its sales have been directed increasingly toward products like automotive brake linings, pipe, siding and paper used principally by the construction industry.
If we refer also, Mr. Speaker, to figures issued by the dominion bureau of statistics for this year, we note important facts. This year production has increased as foreseen, and in relation to previous years; shippings have also increased, except in January.
According to volume 28, No. 1, of the dominion bureau of statistics for January 1959, including asbestos statistics, total production and shippings reached 54,668 tons, as compared to 57,450 tons in January 1958.
For the year 1959 exclusive of December, Canadian deliveries to foreign markets reached a total of 978,655, as compared with 862,550 tons for the same 11-month period in 1958.
This trend towards increased production and increased deliveries, both on the domestic market-which is small-and on the external market-which is considerable-had been forecast in the Gordon report. However, competition on the foreign market has grown, mainly due to asbestos mines in Russia.
I personally know that our mining operators have been trying to find new markets, and that their agents have been covering the world in an attempt to open up new markets; however, Russia now sells large quantities of asbestos on the European markets, so it is hard for Canadian industry to maintain, and even more to increase its trade. I also know that from time to time agents from the Department of Trade and Commerce call on our asbestos industries to collect information on the subject.
However, it is my impression that co-operation between this section of Canadian industry and the departments concerned is inadequate.


It is also my impression that our foreign agents do not have enough contacts with our dealers or with prospective buyers.
The trend towards increased production must surely have been known to the people in charge of our external trade, because it was anticipated in the Gordon report and was also expected by experts in the mineral industry division of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
Do the experts of the Department of Trade and Commerce have frequent enough contacts with the industry in general and with the asbestos industry in particular, to try to forecast production in the years ahead? It would seem that they do not, for this year, as last year, asbestos workers had to be laid off for a few months. There is a foreign trade problem which must be studied by the department.
Personally, I suggest that contacts be established by the officers of the department with all the components of the Canadian industry in order to promote our foreign markets. More frequent contacts should also be made between our official representatives in foreign countries and the representatives or salesmen of the Canadian industry in the countries which do trade with ours. As a matter of fact, and to sum up my opinion, our consulate agents should be travelling salesmen rather than diplomats.
I hope such contacts, which have been lacking in the past, will exist in the future and will produce results. Canada is the major world producer of asbestos and must remain so. It is only through sincere cooperation between the government, asbestos producers and our foreign markets that the asbestos industry can hope to retain the position it has always held in Canada's economy.

Before resuming my seat I should like to explain the attitude which this party will take when we divide in a few minutes time on the motion now before the house. I was asked by my leader to make this statement on his behalf.
Normally, we would accept the formal motion to adopt the address in reply to the speech from the throne out of respect to the throne itself. However, in view of the fact that the government has shown so little respect for the throne as to exclude from the address very important matters of government policy which were introduced in this

debate later by the Prime Minister, we feel that on this occasion we must express our strong disapproval of this procedure and our condemnation of the government's attitude by voting against the motion.

speechtext:
At the outset I should like to associate myself with the others who have spoken in this debate by extending my congratulations to you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, on your appointment to your high office, and also to the mover and seconder of the address.
Among the announcements contained in the speech from the throne is one to which all hon. members must attach great importance-the announcement that a department will be created to concern itself with affairs relating to forestry in Canada. A great part of the Canadian economy depends largely on forest products and the need for conservation in this field is great. It is not my intention to elaborate on this aspect of our economy as others are far more qualified to do so. Indeed, I am not qualified at all.
However, conservation ties in with what I consider a very vital question and one to which I would ask the government to pay close attention, namely the difficulties confronting the Nova Scotia coal industry. Coal is the lifeblood of many towns in my constituency and surrounding areas, towns such as Glace Bay, New Waterford and Dominion. For a number of years, miners have been faced with grave uncertainty and I should like to ask all hon. members of this house to give them the consideration they deserve rather than to take advantage of their plight for the sake of political expediency.
The hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) recently made a trip into my constituency. The coal critic of the official opposition as advertised in the Cape Breton Post of December 10 offering the people of Cape Breton some straight facts. Mr. Speaker, there are some straight facts that are not in possession of the representatives of the men. But I do not hesitate to say that the official opposition coal critic is not in possession of them either. That is very obvious from the statement appearing in the Cape Breton Post by the hon. member following his first look at coal mining as carried on in Cape Breton. It is as follows:
I was terribly impressed by the extension of coal mining as I witnessed it in No. 26 colliery this morning. I am not surprised now at the cost of producing Cape Breton coal and I can easily realize why the industry is facing such a crisis.
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis
This does not tie in with the hon. member's former statement in which he placed the blame on this government. In his speech he advocated a more intensive research program to find more extensive uses for coal, something which, as he is well aware, all the Nova Scotia members are asking. He also advocated a more flexible use of subventions to move coal to markets, a matter in which this government has far surpassed any efforts made by the previous Liberal administration.
The hon. member criticizes the government, and myself for supporting the government, and accuses us of preventing a debate on coal from taking place. At the time the motion was made he was well aware of the fact that it was out of order, but that does not mean a thing. What he fails to realize is that any such criticism must also be directed at the union executives, mayors, councillors and other interested citizens from the mining areas who attended the coal conference when a committee was suggested, which they agreed, was the most logical way to handle the situation. I might also say that among the people present at the coal conference were strong supporters of the hon. member's party and of the C.C.F. party, but as a coal critic he himself was conspicuous by his absence. It is also a well known fact that the hon. member and his party passed up the opportunity to debate the coal issue within a few days of his infamous motion and when it was brought up later he used up the better part of the hour allowed at the time.
Further, his solution-and I quote from page 1574 of Hansard for March 3, 1959-was:
It is true that fewer miners would mean less production, but it would also mean that the problem of the surplus would not be so great and the stock pile would not be so formidable.
Fewer miners, less production, less trouble, Liberal policy.

One more quotation from the Cape Breton Post of December 11:
Mr. Robichaud said he was in Cape Breton largely in the interest of the Liberal party. He explained that because of the lack of Liberals from Nova Scotia circumstances had caused him to become an opposition critic on coal.
There was no mention of personal interest, no mention of the miners and no further mention of the problem. Just circumstances. The hon. member has an approach which is in line with that of the hon. member for betwixt and between, that is, between Newfoundland and Manitoba who, as I understand today, has let the house know that he has now built a house in Newfoundland. There is no mention of whether he is going to make a home there,
670	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis but at least he has a house, which I understand has been under consideration since 1949.
Mr. Hicks, the Liberal opposition leader in Nova Scotia also criticized me for my stand last session, my stand which only agreed with that taken at the coal conference when the committee was suggested and agreed to. Mr. Hicks has a short memory where it applies to Cape Breton miners. His attitude toward the miners during a tie-up in 1956 was different. At that time when meeting with delegations of miners he said, "You do not expect me to forgo my election commitments to meet with you fellows."
I might also say it was not easy to arrange this meeting with Mr. Hicks with what he referred to as "you wildcatters" meaning at the time miners who had been appointed from a union meeting to meet with him. That is the attitude of the Liberal leader in Nova Scotia and his attitude toward coal miners at the time.
This afternoon we heard from the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). What surprises me most about this hon. member is his very short memory. It is not unfair to say that I think he gives me a few years. And speaking of memory, my memory takes me back to 1936, 1937, 1938 and 1939. Speaking from personal experience I can recall working only two days a week. There was no more work for me. I would get $1.50 for that and if I was lucky I would get the second dollar. The hon. gentleman quoted many figures and told us about the unemployment situation. I should like to quote a few figures myself, starting with June of 1936.
It will be noticed that these figures are all for the month of June when unemployment is at its lowest. On June 1, 1936, there were
571.000	unemployed, 12.8 per cent of the labour force; on June 1, 1937, there were
411.000	unemployed, 9.1 per cent of the labour force; on June 1, 1938, there were 522,000 unemployed, 11.4 per cent of the labour force; on June 1, 1939 there were 529,000 unemployed, 11.4 per cent of the labour force; on June 1, 1940, there were 423,000 unemployed, 9.2 per cent of the labour force. It is not surprising he could not recall when he was minister of labour.
As has already been referred to on a couple of occasions in the house today, it is obvious that world war II certainly got the Liberals off the hook and there is no doubt but that the Korean conflict had the same effect for them in 1951.
Any hon. member speaking in the interests of coal and the energy supply of the nation is speaking from a position of strength. This country certainly has plenty of coal. In fact,


the problem faced by Nova Scotia miners is that we have more of it than we can dispose of under present marketing conditions. A recent United States publication states that the proven reserve of petroleum and natural gas hit an all-time high in that country, yet these figures must be considered in comparison to the demands for these products. In other words, the life index of the proven reserves. On the basis of these figures the proven reserves of crude petroleum are equivalent to 12.87 years of production at the present rate. Proven reserves of natural gas have a life index of 22.13 years.
In Canada the picture is not much different. Crude oil and natural gas liquids have a proven reserve of 3.6 billion barrels or a life index of 22 years, while natural gas is in a much more favourable position with a proven reserve of 23.3 trillion cubic feet, or a 150 year life index. However, these natural reserves of the so-called superior fuels do not compare to the life index of our coal reserves. Our proven reserves of coal total 49 billion tons, good for centuries, and the coal reserves of the United States for 800 years at favourable recovery costs, plus another 500 years at costs ranging from 1J to l j times present costs.
It is estimated that even with atomic energy coal will be required to fill from 30 per cent to 40 per cent of the future energy demands in the United States. This puts coal in a very strong position. According to the Chase Manhattan bank the cost of producing a barrel of crude oil has increased 71 per cent in the period between 1948 and 1957, and in all probability will grow steeper.
Canada is rich in natural resources, but the supply is not unlimited. We must utilize wise conservation measures or we will find these resources exhausted, perhaps when we need them most, especially those in short supply, and although I realize that Canada can look forward to further discoveries, this potential is about exhausted in the United States which, in all likelihood, will be turning to our nation for supplies in the future. It therefore follows that wise conservation would serve the national interest best by concentrating the use of each fuel in the market it is best fitted to serve.
Coal has many uses, but it is particularly well suited to serve as a boiler fuel in the utility and heavy industrial field, as well as space heating. Since transportation is one of our greatest problems, I would suggest that markets should be coming to coal. Indeed, the Nova Scotia government has made it attractive to industry setting up in that

province. The electric utilities should establish at the pit head and transmit their power to the heavily populated areas.
The importance of coal in the future has been strongly emphasized of late by the chairman of the Ontario hydro commission and, more recently, by Mr. James G. Macgregor, chairman of the Alberta power commission. Alberta produces more oil and gas than the rest of Canada, yet Mr. Macgregor said:
Alberta power plants, now users of natural gas, are swinging rapidly to coal as more electric power is demanded.
The reason is that big plants can produce more power cheaply by burning coal than they can by burning natural gas at today's prices. I cannot imagine a stronger argument on behalf of coal than this statement made in the province of Alberta.
Mr. Speaker, it is evident that the national security requires a stable and economically sound coal industry, one whose peacetime production base is large enough to permit the expansion necessary to meet accelerated demands of a national emergency. Coal cannot successfully meet such a challenge so long as it is periodically relegated to the role of a standby fuel, and neither could any other energy source.
We have a road to resources program on which we will spend millions. We need roads to our resources. Granted they are underground, but any effort on the part of the government to assist the coal industry to complete plans that have been partially carried out, by completing underground tunnels which will greatly alleviate production costs would be in the interest of the Canadian economy. I will say now that I am grateful to the government for the assistance it made available last year to the coal industry in Nova Scotia and throughout Canada. Whether Dosco has taken advantage of it for this purpose or not I am not aware at the moment, but I know this is a matter for which the union is pressing at home, and especially for the establishment of a coal plant in the area whereby Nova Scotia coal would be made better suited for the market where it is in demand.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I should like also to make some reference to the letter received by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) from Dr. J. H. L. Johnstone, professor of physics at Dalhousie university, regarding the use of Nova Scotia sandstone. The hon. member for Cumberland and I have been in touch with our minister for public works, in the hope that Nova Scotia stone could be used and utilized in the maritime provinces. Dr. Johnstone's letter brings very clearly to our minds what
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis is necessary, and we are very grateful to Dr. Johnstone. It is something to which all Nova Scotians should pay particular attention.
I am quite sure that the very energetic body, APEC, will in the near future, if they have not already done so, be taking action in this regard. Part of Dr. Johnstone's letter reads as follows:
I am interested in the matter not only as a Nova Scotian should he but also because I have been involved during the past two years in the construction of a large university building, in which about 500 tons of Wallace stone have been used.
May I point out that my recent experience leads me to the conclusion that the chief reason why Wallace sandstone is not competitive with stone imported from the United States and central Canada, is that there does not exist in Nova Scotia a modern facility for finishing and cutting the Wallace stone. At the present time, stone has to be forwarded either to New Brunswick or central Canada for finishing, and then returned to Nova Scotia. The exorbitant freight rates (two ways) are such that our stone is not competitive with the imported article.
It appears to me that the solution is to have modern cutting and finishing machinery established at or near the quarry. If this can be done, I feel that Wallace stone can be made competitive.
It has been further pointed out, Mr. Speaker, that not only should this stone be used in Nova Scotia, but it is superior in quality and for that reason efforts should be made to carry out the wishes as expressed by Dr. Johnstone. With respect to the transportation problem, as was indicated in Dr. Johnstone's letter, this Nova Scotian stone has to pay exorbitant freight rates both ways, I am reminded of a statement of President Eisenhower, as quoted by Mr. Arthur Johnstone, president of APEC, in a recent address in Halifax:
Equality of opportunity must be speedily reestablished so that all parts may share proportionately in the productivity of the national economy. As national policy, assistance must be given any group of citizens from whom equality of opportunity is being withheld through no fault of their own.
I appeal to the government to take a close look at the advantages of further promoting our coal industry, in the light of a statement made by Sir Thomas Sopwith who, as head of the Hawker Siddeley Corporation, of which Avro is a part, and Dosco is a subsidiary of Avro, had this to say in his last annual report, published just this week in the Montreal Gazette:
However, in an industrial group such as we have in Canada, results cannot be judged on a year to year basis, and a rather longer view must be taken. We invested in Canada for the future and are confident in the eventual success of our enterprise and the growth of Canada is unimpaired.
This statement came from the president of the Hawker Siddeley Corporation, which, as I indicated, is the parent body of Dosco. It is contrary to those statements being made

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis in the coal industry today. The miners today are not asking for things on a year to year basis, as was indicated by Sir Thomas Sop-with, who indicated they are not operating in Canada on a year to year basis. We are operating on a week to week basis in the Cape Breton coal mines. Coal at one time was the backbone of the whole Dosco enterprise and, until recent years when the policy was adopted that coal stands alone, there was hope that the over-all corporation would carry coal. I feel this is a responsibility that belongs to Dosco. As I pointed out, for years coal was the breadwinner of this organization, and coal continued to carry the other subsidiaries.
In the light of the arguments for the future of coal and the fact that other nations such as Belgium, which has thrown in excess of $61 million into the coal mining areas are taking action, and the statement of Sir Thomas Sopwith, that with the co-operation of the company and governments and the ever-present co-operation of the men, I feel a new deal should be worked out for the coal miners in this country. We in Nova Scotia are certainly part of the Canada and the Canadian future to which Sir Thomas Sopwith refers.
I feel it would be in the interests of the Canadian economy and of the directors and manager of Avro and of Dosco if they would take this statement into consideration which was, as I indicated, just recently published in the Montreal Gazette and possibly in all the other newspapers across the country, in which Sir Thomas Sopwith indicated that their investments in Canada were not made on a year to year basis but that they are looking toward the future, which is certainly what the Cape Breton miners want to do. It is not the future they are looking toward the same as Sir Thomas Sopwith refers to. Their future is only a day, and possibly a week ahead of them. With this attitude that the company has adopted in recent years that coal must stand alone there is the threat hanging over the miners that possibly this week or next week the mines will close.
When speaking of closure, Mr. Speaker, the members of the opposition have made much of the fact that never in the postwar period under a Liberal administration was there a cutback. I will have to agree with them; I will have to go along with the hon. gentlemen that there was not a cutback, but there certainly were closures. Up to 10 mines closed over the period from 1946 to 1956.
